#1198. Diego Kochen shows poise in USMNT net as young goalkeeper stakes claim to starting job

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Historically, goalkeeper has been a position of strength for the United States men's national team, to the extent that during the time of Tim Howard and Brad Guzan, both were playing Premier League soccer, but only one could start between the sticks. Things have changed since then, with numerous keepers coming through the ranks over the years, with most playing domestically or sitting on the bench for stronger European sides. However, that could be coming to an end for the team.

During Mauricio Pochettino's tenure, Matt Freese has been his starting keeper, taking over during the Gold Cup and starting every game that he was available for until the September/October international window, when Pochettino used Diego Kochen and Brian Schwake. Kochen, who is playing his first season of first-team soccer at Lyngby in Denmark (where center back Neil Pierre also got his first taste of senior soccer), got the clean sheet against Mexico during that camp and turned that into a start against Haiti in Concacaf Nations League play in his native Miami, setting the USMNT up well to advance to the semifinals of the tournament.

Following that match, Kochen acknowledged that the USMNT squad has done a lot to put him in this position, and he'll know that even if Pochettino won't be the manager choosing the lineups, performances like this one will be important for how the USMNT keeper picture looks moving forward.

"I feel like I've grown quite a lot," Kochen said following the match, reflecting on his adjustment to the national team. "I'm getting used to competing at the international level, but I've just got to give it to my team because they've been unbelievable. They make it so easy to just come out here and play free and be me, so without them, this wouldn't be possible."

His growth is evident; one of the first things that comes to mind when watching the 20-year-old is his poise. Kochen had the ball at his feet plenty, completing all 20 of his passes to help send the attack on its way, and also made the two saves that he needed to on a mostly quiet night. His age also showed when Haiti scored with him out of position, a goal that was called back for offside, but you take the good with the bad for young players because that's a learning moment, and as he earns more reps at the senior level, those are the kind of mistakes that can be ironed out.

"I'm not saying he hasn't played games in Barcelona, but at the senior level, every game he plays, he gets better and better and better," one of Kochen's coaches, Andreas Bjelland, told CBS Sports. "Because understanding the full-pitch play, and not only being on the line, just taking shots, and being a training goalie, but now he's playing for points every week. He's growing as a player, as a person, and as somebody we can trust more and more in the stuff we do. So it's nice to see that it has come to this ... It's quite impressive."

You can't teach poise, and spending more than five years in the Barcelona system shows in how Kochen carries himself. It's becoming more common in American soccer for young players to test themselves abroad or to get into Major League Soccer teams at a younger age, and when they succeed, it goes a long way developmentally, as Kochen's case shows.

"He is a person who trusts himself a lot. That's also why he's a good goalie, that at such a young age he hasn't that big of a doubt of himself," Mikkel Jespersen, Lyngby's other coach said. "He knows what he's capable of doing, and that's really important as a goalie: that you trust yourself and know what things you are doing is something that can succeed in a longer period."

While it's unknown what the next USMNT manager will value in a keeper, being able to perform in an uncertain environment with your coach having one foot out the door is something that will go a long way for Kochen's chances. In keeper terms, Kochen has plenty of time ahead of him, as players at his position regularly play until their late 30s or early 40s, so if he can continue this trajectory, the question of who protects the net could be solved for the foreseeable future.

Of course, that's a lot of projecting, but when the next generation of the USMNT is developing at an astounding rate, it's only natural to think about where players like Kochen could end up. Doing this in only his first season of professional soccer is already impressive, but the best is yet to come.

#1197. UEFA Women's Champions League Matchday 5: Live stream, schedule what to know as league phase nears end

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There is no more room for error in the 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League. After four matchdays, the league phase has been whittled down to only two games left for each of the 18 clubs, and the margin between a bye into the quarterfinals and an extra round of knockout playoffs in February will come down to dwindling points.

OL Lyonnes rule the league phase at the moment. They top the tournament table with ten points, level with FC Barcelona but with a superior goal difference. Just behind the two Champions League contenders are Bayern Munich and Arsenal, with Chelsea FC and Manchester City creeping closer to the top four. Out of the 18 clubs competing, only four will earn direct berths to the quarterfinals, and eight will compete for a future spot alongside them.

The final six clubs with the least amount of points will see their Champions League dream end, so matchday 5 will be a crucial turning point for several teams.

Fighting for top spot positioning will be Arsenal and OL Lyonnes, and Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain. HB Koge, Roma, and tournament debutants Inter Milan are level on four points and need to be in full urgency mode if they're to leapfrog and remain in contention for future rounds.

Wednesday, Nov. 18BK Hacken vs. Manchester City, 12:45 p.m. (Paramount+)Real Madrid vs. Inter, 12:45 p.m. (Paramount+)   Chelsea vs. Paris Saint-Germain, 3 p.m. (Paramount+)   Juventus vs. OH Leuven, 3 p.m. (Paramount+)  Thursday, Nov. 19 Austria Wien vs. Bayern Munich, 12:45 p.m. (Paramount+)   Paris FC vs. HB Koge, 12:45 p.m. (Paramount+)  Arsenal vs. OL Lyonnes, 3 p.m. (Paramount+)   Barcelona vs. Servette, 3 p.m. (Paramount+)  Benfica vs. Roma, 3 p.m. (Paramount+)

Fans could get a glimpse of a future round when Arsenal take on OL Lyonnes on Thursday. The Gunners now have the tall task of tackling the French giants after battling Barcelona to a 1-1 draw at Camp Nou last week.

A strong team defensive performance, anchored by goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez against the current title holders, and the inclusion of Frida Maanum in the attack were key difference-makers. Manager Renee Slegers and her side seem to be turning the page, with better results after questionable tactics and player availability raised concerns about the club's earlier performances.

Taking on OL Lyonnes also won't be easy. The top French side has scored 20 goals through four league phase matches, and Marie-Antoinette Katoto leads the competition's Golden Boot race with seven goals. U.S. women's national team defensive midfielder Lily Yohannes is getting more lethal in the tournament and scored in her second consecutive tournament match during OL's 6-0 blowout against Juventus.

Lily Yohannes makes it FOUR 💥The USWNT midfielder has now scored in back-to-back UWCL matches 🇺🇸🔥Stream every UEFA Women’s Champions League game on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/9uLM309RM4

The eight-time Champions League winners will go up against an English club with plenty of momentum following last week's results against Barcelona. The Gunners have more players available to shake things up on the pitch, and Alessia Russo remains a threat after her hat trick against Benfica and has four goals in the league phase.

Chelsea FC will host PSG and the Blues are riding high on stout defensive performances. They co-lead the tournament alongside OL Lyonnes with zero goals conceded through four league phase games.

The London side will need to be far better in attack if they want to claim being a top contender, though it's not for lack of trying. They're coming off a scoreless draw against BK Hacken, where they recorded a whopping 32 shots but only six attempts on target. U.S. women's national team winger Alyssa Thompson is still a factor with her swift technique and could help stretch PSG's backline, while Wieke Kaptein gets into dangerous spaces. Kaptein created both goals in Chelsea's 2-0 win against Roma, and the Dutch player has one goal and two assists in the tournament.

PSG's fortunes seem to be turning for the worse after a promising start to the competition. They're in 10th place on the table now with five points and just one win in their last four games. The loss of Sakina Karchaoui with an ankle injury for the remainder of the league phase is a blow to the roster, though Naomie Feller, with two goals and two assists, is a threat for the Parisians.

There are plenty of teams on the lower side of the table and running out of time. Alongside PSG with necessary urgency are Juventus, who were just beaten by OL Lyonnes, 6-0, and face a desperate 17th-place OH Leuven before closing out the league phase against PSG. It makes the penultimate meeting with OH Leuven almost a must win for Juventus, to lessen the stress on the final matchday.

A particularly intriguing matchup between ninth-place Benfica and 12th-place Roma could shake up the league table with a win by either side. If Roma's Kayleigh van Dooren and Alayah Pilgrim stay active on offense again, it could be a tough challenge for Benfica.

#1196. Ordine slams Milan’s Estupiñán: ‘Terror all over his face’

Franco Ordine has launched a stinging attack on Pervis Estupiñán, claiming the Milan full-back is “terrified” of making mistakes in a Rossoneri shirt.

In the Corriere dello Sport, with quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, the veteran journalist used his regular column to look at Milan’s individual performances after Thursday’s 4-2 comeback win at Olympiacos.

“Estupiñán now has a complex about wearing the Milan shirt. Just look at his face when the cameras zoom in on him in key moments: he has terror painted all over it,” Ordine wrote. “And if you’re terrified of making mistakes, it’s mathematically certain that you’ll make them.”

Estupiñán started in Piraeus, where Milan were missing Davide Bartesaghi through injury. However, he was replaced at half-time by Yunus Musah with the Rossoneri trailing 1-0, and Ruben Amorim’s changes then turned the game.

The Ecuadorian joined from Brighton in July 2025 as Theo Hernández’s replacement. He arrived for a reported fee of €17m plus up to €2m in bonuses and add-ons, but has struggled to convince at San Siro.

Ordine was far more positive about Christian Pulisic, who came off the bench to score the winner against Olympiacos.

“Since returning after the World Cup, Pulisic has put together one gem after another, a string of goals each more beautiful and difficult than the last,” he wrote. “Last night’s, the 3-2, was a jewel of technique and precision, as well as instinct in picking the spot where Hutchinson’s pass would arrive.”

It’s not his fault at all……its as a result of a terrible mistake from the coach who instead of allowing the player to move to another club to find a new environment and atmosphere to restart his career elsewhere. Now the decision has back fired. The player’s value will go down, the club will lose money, yet the coach’s ego makes him refuse to admit his error by insisting to play him when it’s obvious that its not working out

#1195. Christian Pulisic bicycle kick sparks USMNT to 2-0 rout of Haiti in Mauricio Pochettino farewell

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In a farewell for Mauricio Pochettino before he heads to Manchester United, the United States men's national team were able to defeat Haiti 2-0 on Tuesday night, advancing in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals 8-0 on aggregate. Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with a bicycle-kick goal to kick things off, which was the emphatic send-off that was needed prior to Pochettino arriving in Manchester, but the USMNT were able to keep things up in the celebration in Cincinnati.

CHRISTIAN PULISIC GET ON YOUR BIKE‼️#USMNT x @VW pic.twitter.com/Yb3yqXfC33

Julian Hall followed with a poacher's goal as Weston McKennie played orchestrator, and it continued a theme that whoever ends up taking over the national team will have tough decisions ahead. Folarin Balogun is struggling for minutes with Monaco and is looking to make a move at the end of the season, and Hall has done everything that he can to increase his own standing with five goals in six games for the USMNT.

The New York Red Bulls star has a ways to go considering that he's still only 18 and will need to gain experience against top teams in the world instead of just Haiti, but he also can't ask for a better start than what he has gotten off to. It's why this is such an attractive job for whoever takes over the USMNT. They'll be able to build upon the good that Pochettino has instilled; the talent is there to move the squad forward, and there's plenty to love about the youth of the USMNT.

And alongside that, Pulisic has essentially screamed don't forget about me. During this camp, the Milan man has followed up on signing a new contract with the club by reaching 35 national team goals, moving into fourth all time for the USMNT over Eric Wynalda. Diego Kochen added to the good vibes with a third straight clean sheet, and Neil Pierre was even able to be cap-tied against the nation that he's also eligible for as the full-circle moments were left and right.

Pulisic, the former 17-year-old phenom, was subbed off for Cavan Sullivan, the current 17-year-old phenom, and while the goal difference may have been larger in the first leg between these sides, this felt like a more measured performance despite the strangeness of Pochettino's assistants heading to United while he managed the squad prior to catching his own charter.

This camp had every chance of being a disaster given the circumstances of Pochettino leaving, but all parties did what was needed during this camp. All dual nationals were capped, including Santiago Castaneda, showing that even on his way out, Pochettino made sure to take care of the future of the federation. On to the next round of the Concacaf Nations League with a new manager and no complaints with the performance so far for the squad.

#1194. Augmenting reality with integrated photonics

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 915–926 (2026) Cite this article

Augmented-reality (AR) glasses promise to transform how we interact with the world by seamlessly blending digital content with our physical surroundings. Yet making them viable for comfortable, all-day use remains deeply challenging, constrained by hard trade-offs of size, power and display performance. This calls for fundamentally new ways to generate and control light with high precision in an ultracompact form factor. Here we examine how integrated photonics can help bridge the technology gap in AR hardware. We review the basics of AR displays and recent advances in integrated photonics for new AR display components and architectures, then turn to key challenges and future directions, from component development to system innovation and scalable manufacturing, and highlight broader opportunities for synergy with fields such as quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

#1193. Pascal Gross interview: Brighton isn't a nice stepping stone club anymore. We're a big club who need to be ruthless - we can win every game

Published: 21:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 26 November 2026

Before Pascal Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler. It was time, he suggested, for the club to take the next step.

‘There were some games in the past where we went (away to big teams) and you're not sure you can really do it,’ Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But we should now have a mindset that we can win every game. I really believe in that. We have the players. That’s what I said.

‘People say we are nice club and, yeah, maybe we are. But on the pitch, it was time to be ruthless. Time to kill games, be a big club. That’s what this is about now.’

Gross may feel his ambition has been vindicated, at least in part. Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death. Gross, 35, ended that one on his knees in his own penalty area, having tried in vain to stop Oli McBurnie sliding in Hull’s second goal.

‘That felt really, really bad,’ he says. ‘Maybe today (Tuesday) is the first day I am starting to feel a bit better about it. I would be more worried if we didn’t create chances. We did. We just didn’t score.’

‘On the pitch, it was time to be ruthless,' Pascal Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Time to kill games, be a big club. That’s what this is about now’

Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death

Before Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler

Brighton are six points behind leaders Arsenal – who they have already beaten 3-0 at the Amex – but are the Premier League’s top scorers by a distance, with 26.

Gross, the German who returned to Sussex after a short spell at Borussia Dortmund, has created an astonishing 31 chances for his team. That puts him only two behind the best in the country this term, his friend and Germany team-mate Florian Wirtz.

The debate about Wirtz’s value or otherwise to Liverpool has swirled around the country since he arrived at Liverpool in the summer of 2025 for £116million. The conversation even reached Brighton’s training ground.

‘Jamie Redknapp was there and he asked me all about it just a couple weeks ago,’ Gross explains. ‘I just told him: "He's too good not to prove himself." People here still don't know how good he is, but they will. He's a complete package and he knows I support him a lot.

‘Football is a team sport. It’s not ever on one person. Also, nobody should forget just how difficult and different the Premier League is when you first come.’

Gross knows this well. He smiles at the mention of his own first English away game – a 2-0 defeat at Leicester in August 2017 that brings to mind the Patrice Evra quote about his first experience of playing in England being akin to ‘an afternoon spent in a washing machine’.

‘I was on the floor so much that day that I looked like a little child,’ Gross recalls. ‘It was just all too physical. I knew I had to improve fast, play faster. My decision-making had to be quicker.

‘My father called me after and said I wouldn’t last three weeks if I played like that again. But I already knew. Going home that day, I really questioned a lot of things. But that’s just how hard it is when you come to the Premier League.’

Gross had a brutal introduction to the Premier League in 2017, but it was a reminder of the level he needed to reach

Gross fires in Brighton's equaliser at Old Trafford in the Carabao Cup back in September. The Seagulls trailed 2-0 but fought back brilliantly to dump out Man United

Brighton players Luka Vuskovic and Groß visit local independent restaurant Riddle & Finns to support American Express' Shop Small campaign

The Hull game was Gross' 300th in a Brighton shirt, and he is perhaps playing at a higher level than ever with four goals and four assists in the first 11 league games this season, as well as a goal in the Carabao Cup win at Manchester United. On an official club podcast, former striker and team-mate Glenn Murray labelled him Brighton's best-ever player, and last week he signed a new contract keeping him on the south coast until the end of next season.

Signed by Chris Hughton from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt after the Seagulls' promotion to the top division a little over nine years ago, Gross has had an inside view of the most successful period in the club’s history.

During his time, Brighton have sold enough players for big profit to make a pretty good Premier League XI – Robert Sanchez, Ben White, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marc Cucurella, Moises Caicedo, Alexis Mac Allister, Leandro Trossard and Joao Pedro get you most of the way there, for a total transfer taking of £424m. Gross suspects there will be more over time.

Equally, he feels the days of players using Brighton as a stepping stone to the next level are gone. A lack of commitment soon gets sniffed out, he says.

‘There have been players who saw it like that,’ he explains. ‘And they couldn't even get in our team because they came with the wrong mindset. If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team.

‘And if you do come with the right mentality and you push every day, and the team is doing well, I always say that good things will come for everybody – for the club, for the coaches, for the players.

‘I love the club, and we have big potential. There will always be players that move on. But I think the players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a big club in the Premier League. We have been there almost 10 years and are improving all the time.’

Gross thought hard before first leaving Germany for England. He visited Brighton’s training ground twice before making his decision and, once he had, dug down into the individual statistics of the players who would soon be team-mates.

Gross (right) has seen a huge change at Brighton since joining from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt, where he played under former Southampton manager Ralph Hasenhuttl (left)

Brighton's form this season has been inspired by a prolific attack, with their 26 Premier League goals by far the most in the division

They have progressed season on season despite the departure of a host of star players for big money, including Alexis Mac Allister (right) to Liverpool for £35m in 2023

Having married and had two children in Sussex, Gross has the club in his heart and soul now. We meet to talk at beachfront restaurant Riddle & Finns as part of American Express’s Shop Small campaign, encouraging people to support local business.

During his spell at Dortmund – who he adored as a boy – Gross watched every Brighton game on TV. But it may not have been this way. There was a time, in pre-season 2020, when former Brighton manager Graham Potter told Gross he could leave.

‘That was hard to take,’ Gross says. ‘I asked him if there was no chance at all of me playing. I needed to know if he saw me as, like, No17 or 18 in the squad so that whatever I did, I wouldn't play. Or in his mind was I 12, 13 or 14?

‘Then I figured I could work my way back into the team because I would always back myself to prove the manager wrong. We lost a lot of games and eventually, I came back into the team.’

Gross’s approach back then was to train as well and as hard as he could. Murray recalls that his attitude stood out.

‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense.’

Culture is often discussed in modern football but it’s just a new word for an old truth: unhappy football teams tend to fail.

‘There are days when you see, maybe, that the way we play gives an opponent frustration and you can see bad body language,’ Gross says. ‘That's where I sense we have them.

‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross, pictured celebrating the win at Man City with Jack Hinshelwood. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense’

'If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team'

'Players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a big club in the Premier League'

‘But there are also teams who maybe struggle but they are still together and they're still fighting and you see a group of guys who can still be hard to beat. That’s about culture. It’s important and I think we value that here.’

As part of Brighton’s leadership group, Gross speaks regularly to manager and compatriot Hurzeler. His personal creed is that confidence should never bleed into arrogance – ‘I just hate that’ – and he believes that Hurzeler, known to rub the occasional manager up the wrong way, is on the right side of the line.

‘He is pushing, pushing,’ Gross says with a smile. ‘He has so much passion for the job, he puts so much work into it. He wants to challenge, he wants to think differently.

‘He doesn't want to think: “Everything is nice." He really wants to push himself and us. And that balance is a really fine balance. He's trying to stretch the limit and I think that's good.’

Pascal Gross is supporting American Express Shop Small, which aims to support small businesses by encouraging the nation to back their local high street on Small Business Saturday and beyond. This year, American Express is investing £1million in new Shop Small grants, offering 100 independent UK businesses £10,000 each to help them grow, innovate and invest in their future. Visit go.amex/shopsmalluk

#1191. Raimondo makes speedy recovery ahead of Frosinone vs. Parma

Antonio Raimondo has returned from injury well ahead of schedule and is in Frosinone’s squad for Saturday’s Serie A clash with Parma.

According to Corriere dello Sport, the striker is one of 26 players called up by Massimiliano Alvini for the game at the Stadio Benito Stirpe, which kicks off at 15:00 CET [14:00 GMT]. Midfielder Florian Grillitsch has also recovered and is in the squad.

Raimondo injured his left ankle in Frosinone’s win over Torino on 1 November, and tests revealed a contusion-sprain injury with damage to several ligaments in the ankle. At the time, the estimated recovery time was around a month and a half, which would have kept him out until mid-December.

His return comes at a good time for Alvini’s side. The Gialloazzurri have lost both games they’ve played without him, including Sunday’s 5-1 defeat at Milan.

The 22-year-old has been one of the stories of the season so far. He has eight goals in 11 Serie A appearances and another in the Coppa Italia, and his form has helped Frosinone climb to seventh.

#1190. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Thierno Barry puts Everton ahead after Tyrique George's shot isn't dealt with by Lukáš Horníček! 🔵 https://t.co/oRXsrwbOhz

Everton had the lead and it was so easy and straightforward. They waited for Newcastle to give the ball away and then broke at speed. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was superb and forced a fingertip save from Hornicek. From the resulting corner, Hornicek was needed again to keep out Jake O’Brien’s header.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

"HOW did it not go in?" Newcastle came inches from an equaliser 🤯 https://t.co/N0DJuk9BLZ

Their final chance fell to Yoane Wissa, whose shot on the turn was saved by the feet of Jordan Pickford. All that was left was for Jacob Ramsey to get himself sent off, with two yellow cards in the space of 86 seconds.

Jacob Ramsey sees red after coming on as a second-half substitute 🟥 https://t.co/26t7GkRdcg

“Lots of the game it was [one of their best performances]. We probably had better chances in the first half. [Not taking them] kept it really difficult. Getting the first goal was important. Incredibly proud of the team all the time because their effort is unquestionable. There is not a lot of them but they are doing a great job and hope it continues.

“We are creating chances, that is the big thing for me. Thierno [Barry] has had some big opportunities. He was on the spot today. I was worried ‘was he on or offside at the time?’. I do not think anyone enjoys playing the same team twice so quickly. So for us to win both is hugely important for us. We want to get back to the top end of the league, it is incredibly tight.”

“I think it was probably our best performance of the season, I thought we were terrific in the first half and could have scored two or three. Thierno [Barry] gets the goal again for us. There is a lot on his shoulders, he is our only recognised striker so hopefully he can keep putting the ball in the net like he has done. He is harsh on himself but his numbers are through the roof in terms of running. A clean sheet is massive for us. It is a long old season. We take it game by game but tonight feels good and we can look forward to Friday [against Coventry].”

"One of our best performances of the season" Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall reacts to his side's big away win 👏 https://t.co/vfcNmIIDGf

The final whistle is blown at St James’ Park and Everton claim all three points thanks to Barry’s goal early in the second half. Everton go up into seventh with this win, with Newcastle down in 13th. There are a lot of boos at the sound of the final whistle. A lot of forlorn faces on the Newcastle players.

That probably sums up the night for Newcastle as they are down to 10 men. Ramsey had only just been booked moments before and is now given his marching orders for a nasty challenge on Armstrong. He can have no complaints and that is complete stupidity from Ramsey.

Jacob Ramsey sees red after coming on as a second-half substitute 🟥 https://t.co/26t7GkRdcg

Ramsey fouls Hackney and is booked for that late challenge.

Some of the home faithful have decided they have seen enough and are heading for the exits.

Everton have negotiated half of the time added on.

A late change for Everton as Hackney comes on for George.

Wissa should equalise for Newcastle. Toure’s cutback from the byline picks out Wissa in the centre of the penalty area. Wissa takes a touch on the spin before getting a shot away but he is denied by the legs of Pickford.

There will be eight minutes of added time so Newcastle do still have plenty of time to find an equaliser.

"There was the chance for Newcastle!" Jordan Pickford keeps out Yoane Wissa 🧤 https://t.co/dsHX03CEtE

A final change for Newcastle sees Toure, with a piece of paper, replace Dedic. Schar took a quick look and then just tossed it to the ground.

Newcastle’s first shot on target of the game comes from Wissa 85 minutes into the game but it is a tame effort from range that rolls into Pickford’s arms.

Murphy swings in a cross from the right and picks out Osula but the latter’s header a fair way out from goal goes wide of the far post.

A change at the back for Everton as Keane replaces Branthwaite.

Ramsey comes close to an equaliser. Dedic lays it off to Ramsey, who strikes it first time just outside the box, but his effort goes inches wide of the post.

Everton have taken off Barry and he is replaced by Johnson.

Barry bundles over Schar to gift Newcastle a free-kick not far outside the Everton penalty area. Before it is taken, Newcastle are making another double change. Murphy and Ramsey replace Elanga and Joelinton.

Barnes clips it in towards the far post looking for Osula but O’Brien heads away.

David Moyes has been booked for encroaching onto the pitch.

That is a huge interception from Schar. Rohl drives down Everton’s right and spots the run of Barry into the box. He sends in the cross but Schar slides in to intercept. But did he go through the back of Barry to get to the ball? The VAR checks and decides that Schar got the ball first. The more you look at the replays when you really slow them down it appears that Schar might have made contact with Barry’s leg before the ball but it probably is not definitive enough to overturn the original, on-field decision.

Newcastle want a penalty as Hall goes down under a challenge from Rohl but is there enough in that to give a penalty? Probably not as VAR checks and clears the incident. It was a delayed reaction from Hall, who if he had gone down immediately after the contact may have changed the VAR’s mind.

How have Newcastle not scored there? Barnes’ cross from the left comes all the way to the back post, where Elanga looks destined to score but somehow he does not as his effort hits the post and does not cross the line. That was probably harder to miss than to score as Elanga was about a yard away from the goal.

"HOW did it not go in?" Newcastle came inches from an equaliser 🤯 https://t.co/N0DJuk9BLZ

Unsurprisingly, Matthias Jaissle is turning to his bench. It is a double change as Steur and Wissa replace Gonzalez and Willock.

The space opens up for Dewsbury-Hall in a central position around 25 yards out and he decides to shoot. He tries to curl one into the top corner and his effort is tipped over the bar by Hornicek.

From the subsequent corner, Garner’s delivery goes beyond the back post and picks out the head of O’Brien, whose header nearly sneaks in at the near post but is denied by the arm of Hornicek.

Elanga’s cross from the right finds Willock in the penalty area. Willock probably takes too many touches with too many players crowded around him and he is unable to get a proper, dangerous shot away.

It would be no surprise to see Matthias Jaissle turn to his bench imminently. On Thursday in the cup, he made a triple change at the break.

Everton come close to a second. A cross is sent in by George from the right and comes all the way to the back post. Branthwaite has the advantage massively height wise over Hall and wins the header, forcing Hornicek into the save.

Everton can smell a second goal with Newcastle all over the place. The home fans were hoping for a reaction after half-time but it has not happened for the hosts, who have not been at the races all night.

David Moyes’ side squandered some chances in the first half but they take the lead early in the second. Everton take a free-kick inside the Newcastle half quickly before Dewsbury-Hall slides an incisive pass into the box to pick out the run of George. He opens up his body and gets his shot away but it is too close to Hornicek. The Newcastle goalkeeper should do so much better but lets it slip underneath him, allowing Barry to have a simple tap-in to put Everton in front.

VAR is going to take a look at two possible offsides with both George and Barry under the spotlight. The Newcastle fans will be hoping for a reprieve here. The first one is cleared and so is the second so the goal will stand. You cannot say that Everton do not deserve to be in front. The Newcastle players also felt that Barry had fouled Schar in the build-up but the officials do not agree.

Thierno Barry puts Everton ahead after Tyrique George's shot isn't dealt with by Lukáš Horníček! 🔵 https://t.co/oRXsrwbOhz

The weather in the north east has certainly taken a turn for the worse with the rain hammering down.

We are back under way at St James’ Park as the rain begins to fall. You would assume that Newcastle will not be as poor in this second half as they were in the first. Will Everton live to regret not taking a few good chances in that first half?

“They [Newcastle] have been poor, and the supporters have let them know how poor they have been. Everton have been far the better side. David Moyes will be pleased but disappointed that they are not 1-0 in front.”

Possession: Newcastle 50%-50% EvertonShots: 5-10Shots on target: 0-0Corners: 2-0Touches in opposition box: 8-17

Armstrong should probably put Everton in front with the last kick of the half but misses the target. Dewsbury-Hall cuts the ball back from the left to pick out the run of Armstrong into the penalty area. From the penalty spot, Armstrong opens up his right foot to try and guide it into the far corner but his effort goes just wide.

That is the final act of the half and it remains goalless at St James’ Park. Some boos ring around the stadium as the players head off.

That is a good late chance in the half for Everton. Dewsbury-Hall clips a dangerous ball in from the left and picks out O’Brien at the back post but the defender cannot guide his header on target. That was whilst Hall was still off and Barnes was operating as a temporary left-back.

Hall has received some treatment to his back and is now back to his feet.

Hall has stayed down after Barry collided into the back of the Newcastle left-back going up for a header.

George is dispossessed inside his own half before Willock plays it forward to Joelinton. The Brazilian takes one touch before shooting from just outside the box but his effort flies wide of Pickford’s left post. Joelinton struck it powerfully but cut cross the ball too much.

Barnes cuts inside from the left and drives across the face of the penalty area. His shot is semi-blocked by Branthwaite and loops into the air towards his own goal. Pickford takes no risks and palms it over his own bar. Hall’s delivery is headed on by Burn but then cleared by Mykolenko.

Garner is the one to take it but his effort is blocked by the wall. He tried to beat Hornicek at his near post rather than go completely over the wall but the end of the wall still blocks it.

Barry is fouled by Burn just outside the Newcastle penalty area and the latter is the first player into the book tonight. Burn protests his innocence but replays show that the referee was 100% correct with his decision. Burn is a touch fortunate that it is just outside the box. Garner and Dewsbury-Hall are stood over this one...

I would say that the Newcastle fans have gone from frustrated to now quite annoyed with how their side has begun this game. Plenty of groans and moans inside St James’ Park; their only relief will be that they are not behind.

David Moyes will be desperate to see his side score and take advantage of Newcastle not being at the races. The frustration from the home fans continues to grow and this is Everton’s opportunity. You cannot imagine that Newcastle will be this poor throughout the game.

That is a glorious chance for Barry that he should really have taken. A free-kick is sent into the Newcastle box and Branthwaite wins the header. The ball falls to Barry who, from ten yards out, has a big chance to put Everton in front but instead it is more of an air shot. In fact, he ends up kicking Osula to gift Newcastle a free-kick.

Rohl has Everton’s first proper sighting of goal tonight but he wastes the opportunity from the right side of the box, failing to keep his shot down and sees it go over Hornicek’s bar.

We are seeing many of the same issues with Newcastle United’s so-called vertical football under Matthias Jaissle already this evening.

Aimless long balls to nobody hoisted forward. Long balls aimed at someone who fails to win the first header or challenge and possession is given back to Everton.

There have already been a few grumbles from the home crowd as William Osula is sent off on another forlorn chase of an over-hit pass in behind the Everton centre backs.

We are nearly 20 minutes into the game and Everton striker Barry is still yet to touch the ball.

Joelinton’s shot from the edge of the box is struck powerfully and is blocked by Tarkowski, going behind for Newcastle’s first corner of the night. Hall’s delivery beyond the back post finds Burn but his header from just a few yards out goes wide. Burn should really be hitting the target from so close to the goal.

We are just a quarter of an hour into this one but you can already sense some frustration from the home fans. Everton, despite being away from home, have settled well into this game.

To sum up the frustration from the home supporters, Dedic plays a dreadful long free-kick into the box that has far too much on it and goes behind.

Under the lights at home, you would assume Matthias Jaissle would have wanted a fast start from his side but that has not happened for the hosts.

Barnes is afforded space to cut inside from the left and, from the corner of the penalty area, clips a dangerous ball towards the far post. There is slightly too much on it and the ball goes behind for a goal-kick, although for a moment Pickford appeared to be panicking. That is the second time Barnes has been given too much space to cut inside and if Everton keep allowing that, you would imagine that they will eventually be punished.

The two starting XIs are fairly similar to the ones that started on Thursday night but the obvious difference between the League Cup tie and tonight’s Premier League encounter is the change of ground. How big an impact can the Newcastle fans have on the outcome of this one?

Unsurprisingly, former Sunderland goalkeeper Pickford is roundly booed by the home crowd upon his first touch.

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday this coming weekend, with this being Newcastle’s final home league game before then, St James’ Park pauses to remember all those who have given their lives to protect this country. The Last Post is played after St James’ Park falls silent.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off from St James’ Park. Here is a reminder of how the sides line up this evening:

Newcastle: Hornicek; Dedic, Schar, Burn, Hall; Joelinton, Gonzalez; Elanga, Willock, Barnes; Osula.Substitutes: Pope, Botman, Bamba, Wissa, Thiaw, Steur, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey.

Everton: Pickford; O’Brien, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong, Dewsbury-Hall; Rohl, George, Barry. Substitutes: Travers, Maitland-Niles, Dibling, Keane, Johnson, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Graham.

“I think everybody who has been in football and comes to St James’ Park knows what the atmosphere is like here. We have to try and quell it the best way we can. Newcastle have got some really good players. It is a Premier League game, we know a lot about them, they know a lot about us. I do not think there are too many big surprises tonight.”

“We picked up on what we can do better [against Everton], this is something we focused on in training, really committed in the last few days so hopefully we can deliver today.”

On Anthony Elanga returning to the starting line-up:

“It is important now after he was out for a long time with an injury. Now he is improving a lot physically and also getting the feeling to play with the lads again. Therefore he deserves to start today and hopefully he can put his potential on the pitch.”

On Will Osula starting after an injury scare:

“He is such a talented guy, young lad, he can cause any opposition problems so hopefully he can deliver that again with his strength.”

On what he is hoping for tonight to get the three points:

“Be clinical, ruthless in both boxes. Defend with everything you have and then be efficient and use every opportunity to score and then I think we will see a great result today.”

“That helps us for sure. The extra motivation and extra energy will be there from the stands and that is something that we can always count on here at home in our stadium.”

“Nothing more than what I am sure you have already heard so he is not in the team tonight.”

"A pretty decent start!" 🔵 Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall discusses Everton's start to the season and where he feels they need to improve. https://t.co/alCMsgoH0j

This was going to be a younger, more dynamic squad that would grow with the club as they looked to live up to the promise made by David Hopkinson, the chief executive, that they would be “consistently and credibly challenging” for top honours in England and Europe by 2030.

Having sold Bruno Guimarães (£73m), Sandro Tonali (£90m) and Anthony Gordon (£67m), Newcastle were able to spend roughly £262.9m on eight players to reinvigorate the squad as they once again talked about challenging for European qualification in Matthias Jaissle’s first season as manager.

Newcastle are 12th in the Premier League, but have had an inconsistent start and there are concerns that too many of these signings have failed to shine. Jaissle is leaning heavily on the players he inherited from Howe instead.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. #1189. USWNT roster for Concacaf W Championship: Ashley Sanchez back, Sam Coffey returns, and Naomi Girma misses out

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest roster of the year for the U.S. women's national team is here. Head coach Emma Hayes has named a 23-player roster for the upcoming 2026 Concacaf W Championship.

The tournament serves as the World Cup qualifiers, and four teams will earn spots in the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, with future Olympic spots also in play. Fans can watch all the Concacaf W Championship matches on Paramount+.

In just nine short days, eight teams will compete in a quarterfinal round. The U.S. and Canada earned direct byes into the tournament as Concacaf's top two ranked teams, and six teams now join them after a preliminary qualifying round. The USWNT will face El Salvador on Nov. 27 in the quarterfinal round, and if they advance, they'll clinch a spot in next year's World Cup. The other matchups are Canada against Panama, Mexico vs. Haiti, and Jamaica will play Costa Rica.

"It's been a great year of growth and learning for our team, and for a long time the focus has been on qualifying for the World Cup, so now that time has arrived," said Hayes.

"I want to see relentless consistency from our players, individually and as a team, and I want us to be elite in both penalty boxes. If we can achieve that, I'm confident those performances will carry us through to meet our standards and goals. This is my first Concacaf event and the first for many of our players, so we're all looking forward to the experience."

Hayes selected a full roster that features several players competing in their first-ever senior-level World Cup qualifying tournament, and a handful of veterans. Just eight of the 23 players selected were members of the 2022 Concacaf W Championship roster: forwards Mallory Swanson, Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson, and Ashley Sanchez; defender Emily Fox; and midfielders Lindsey Heaps, Rose Lavelle, and Sam Coffey -- who joined mid-tournament that year.

Coffey returns to the roster after missing two previous international windows while managing a lower-leg injury. Defender Naomi Girma is out as she continues to manage a lingering calf injury. The centerback has not featured with the national team since April, and has yet to play with Chelsea FC this season. Midfielder Olivia Moultrie is currently rehabbing from an ACL injury sustained in August. Other notable omissions on the roster are Jaedyn Shaw and Ally Sentnor, both of whom have been part of U23 and senior camps throughout the year.

This is just the third camp for the attacking line of "triple espresso" since the 2024 Olympics. If the trio starts a match during the Concacaf W Championship, it will be the first time they start a game together since the gold medal match. Both Swanson and Wilson have worked their way back into senior camps over the year following maternity leave.

Goalkeepers (3): Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign FC; 12/0), Mandy McGlynn (Utah Royals FC; 6/0), Phallon Tullis-Joyce (Manchester United, ENG; 8/0)

Defenders (8): Tierna Davidson (Gotham FC; 72/3), Kate Del Fava (Utah Royals FC; 1/0), Emily Fox (Arsenal FC, ENG; 80/1), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash; 15/1), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit; 12/0), Evelyn Shores (Angel City FC; 0/0), Gisele Thompson (Angel City FC; 12/0), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave FC; 9/1)

Midfielders (6): Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current; 7/1), Sam Coffey (Manchester City, ENG; 46/5), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit FC; 180/40), Claire Hutton (Bay FC; 22/1), Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC; 124/29), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes, FRA; 22/1)

Forwards (6): Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current; 16/1), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit; 59/13), Ashley Sanchez (North Carolina Courage; 30/4), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars; 105/39), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea FC, ENG; 34/4), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns FC; 65/25)

Ashley Sanchez's return to the roster comes after standout performances against Spain last window and a stellar 2026 NWSL regular season where she won the Golden Boot with 20 goals scored. She was also nominated for the 2026 NWSL MVP award. A positional shift to left winger and an outrageous amount of scoring have all led her back to the USWNT due to consistent performances, a key factor for Hayes with her large player pool.

"Be consistent first of all in performance. Ashley Sanchez wasn't on our radar, not because she isn't talented, but there were certain things we demanded from the performance that I think she has delivered in her game on a regular basis. So, I think that's the first thing. I think you've seen that includes Croix Bethune coming into this camp -- been outstanding in the number 10 position all year, and would have been in last camp as well if she was fit. You do have to consistently find consistent performances, particularly if you're a player that doesn't have credit in the bank," Hayes said.

As the World Cup gets nearer, finalizing a roster for the 2027 summer tournament is even closer. Things like consistent form and senior-level experience will come into play when naming a final 23 for the World Cup for Hayes.

"If you're a Mallory Swanson and delivered on a world stage on a regular basis for the national team, it does alter things slightly. No, we don't want players that are in our group that are in a place where they're not fighting to improve every day or be as competitive as they could possibly be, but I think when players have stacked and accumulated a lot of experience over a period of time, that is always going to put them in a steady position," Hayes explained.

"But it doesn't guarantee anything. I will be unafraid to leave anybody off that plane if I don't feel that they are applying themselves to put ourselves in the best possible position to compete. Which is why this upcoming camp, our job is to qualify for the World Cup, and so everything we have worked towards is ensuring that every player that comes in at camp makes sure they lift their level and they position the team to have the most positive outcome, regardless of the opponent. And I'd be demanding as much as I always do, but I have a big expectation from our senior players to step up."

El Salvador is the eighth-ranked team in the Concacaf W Championship and earned its spot following a preliminary qualifying round. The group is coached by manager Eric Acuña, who recently made headlines for harshly criticizing his players in a press conference following losses to Paraguay last month.

Still, Hayes and the staff aren't taking any opponent lightly no matter the rankings or state of the locker room.

"It's a team that knows is competing for something, so it doesn't matter the opponent; they're competing to go to a World Cup, and do I think that will be it will be demanding and taxing? And yes, I do. In many different ways, because the expectations are all on us. I think for them, it's how are they going to disrupt us and make it difficult? But they have two players in the front line that can cause a lot of problems, particularly in transition. So we have to set up for that," Hayes said.

"I think when it when it comes to the players, I've always championed creating positive environments for players. And yeah, I'm sad for the players to hear what they've gone through, but as always, I can't control that. I want the best for players all of the time in their environments, but I am here to represent the U.S. and try and help us qualify for the World Cup. So my focus is on that. Even if my heart goes out to the players and I think we still have a lot of work to do in the women's game to keep driving female-centered, female-lens environments where women can thrive."

Milan have rekindled their interest in Fenerbahçe left-back Archie Brown as they consider their options on the left flank.

According to MilanNews24, the Rossoneri are studying the Englishman’s situation again, more than a year after he turned them down. Brown chose Fenerbahçe over Milan in July 2025, when the Turkish club bought him from Gent for €8 million and signed him until June 2028, with an extra year as an option.

Brown came through Derby County’s academy before spells at Lausanne-Sport and Gent.

#1187. Why U.S. Soccer's move to name Emma Hayes to the USMNT hiring committee makes sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – By the time U.S. Soccer confirmed Mauricio Pochettino's departure for Manchester United early Friday morning, the announcement itself was far from a surprise. The press release included the usual formalities – Steve Cherundolo, the U-23 U.S. men's national team head coach, would fill in for the Dec. 13 friendly against Jamaica that falls outside the FIFA international match calendar, and the assurance that the search for Pochettino's USMNT successor would begin shortly. Federation CEO J.T. Batson and COO Dan Helfrich will unsurprisingly lead the search, as will "the soccer leadership team at U.S. Soccer that includes" assistant sporting director Oguchi Onyewu. There was one unique detail tucked into the announcement, though.

Emma Hayes, the U.S. women's national team head coach, will also have a say in the matter.

Men's and women's national teams rarely overlap at any given federation, largely because there's little need for a crossover event. They operate on different calendars and in the best case scenarios, each team has dedicated members of staff. Hayes' name-drop as news of Pochettino's exit became official, then, is a unicorn-like sighting, even if U.S. Soccer often champions a spirit of collaboration between all of its national teams. It is uncommon for the head coach of one senior national team to help recruit a counterpart but in U.S. Soccer's case, it makes complete sense.

Hayes' coaching career, which spans two decades and two continents, means her inclusion on the federation's soccer leadership team is an obvious one. She is amongst the most respected soccer minds in the game, which easily makes her one of the most important people on U.S. Soccer's payroll no matter how you look at it. That will be especially true in a hiring process that has to conclude with a compelling follow-up act to Pochettino's splashy arrival two years ago. Her perspective might actually be vital in the process, which only adds to the intrigue of what's next for the USMNT.

"We have an extraordinary gift, which is a women's national team manager who's incredibly insightful, bright mind about the sport, who has a set of personal experiences and relationships that span the club and international game, the men's and women's game, the domestic and international club game, and who also has lived in the shoes of what it's like to be a U.S. national team senior coach," Helfrich told CBS Sports on Thursday. "It is a no-brainer that that mind and that voice has a really prominent seat at the table when we're talking about important moves for the federation."

USMNT coaches are rarely style hires; look no further than the list of people to hold the job on a full-time basis this century and the picture paints itself. The only thing Bruce Arena, Bob Bradley, Jurgen Klinsmann, Gregg Berhalter and Pochettino seem to have in common, outside of the job they all once held, is that they were all tasked with some sort of cultural reset depending on the task at hand. That likely will not be the case for Pochettino's successor, though, who will inherit a team with a clear style of play, a healthy mix of veteran players and rising talents and plenty of time on the clock until the next World Cup. The job will be defined in part by continuity, even with the necessary allowance for the new hire to put their unique spin on things.

That's where Hayes' expertise should play a crucial role, and the same goes for Onyewu. Hayes' tactical know-how makes her as qualified as anyone employed by U.S. Soccer to establish the right stylistic profile for the next USMNT coach, especially with the spirit of continuity in mind. Pochettino's track record with the U.S. team was mixed but at its best, his high-intensity, attack-minded approach suited the player pool really well and continues to do so. Hayes, a tactical pragmatist who prioritized attack-minded teams herself with Chelsea and the USWNT, will be more than able to help match candidates to the player pool they will spend the next several years working with. Hayes admitted as much on Wednesday when addressing the topic for the first time.

"I work really closely with J.T. in particular and even more so with Dan as we're growing to develop the American soccer movement and J.T. asked if I would be involved as a technical voice, to be involved with the process and I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men's national team coach," she said. "My role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job, albeit with the women's team, and that I've coached for a number of years and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why and like I said, I feel confident in the group that are being put together. I think it'll be a very thorough process. I think that's the most important part of it and like I said, I feel very embedded in what we're doing with the federation so it doesn't feel unusual to me so, like I've said many times, let's build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that's the important part and let's get it right."

That's especially true considering the fact that there are very few slam-dunk candidates to replace Pochettino. Pep Guardiola, months into a sabbatical after a decade with Manchester City, is an obvious target for U.S. Soccer but it is entirely unclear how interested he would be in the vacancy. If he's out of the running, the list of contenders with genuine international appeal dwindles quickly but it does not necessarily mean the list of worthy candidates vanishes with Guardiola. The hiring committee will need to be strategic in that case, both in terms of creating a list of contenders and then narrowing them down over the interview process, Hayes providing an important perspective along the way.

The jobs of the USMNT and the USWNT head coaches are hardly apples-to-apples but even then, one will still have an acute idea of what the other's job entails. There is inherent value in having a coach help in the process of hiring another coach, since they hold such singular positions – they are often treated as the be-all, end-all when it comes to their team's success, fairly or otherwise. She can also speak to the cadence of national teams, which varies greatly from the club game where coaches essentially work with their players every day during a long season.

"Everyone is aware of the major differences between coaching at the club level and international level, and the main difference is just time on the field and time with your players," Hayes told CBS Sports earlier this year when asked about Pochettino. "Every international coach would love to have more time with their team, but that's not the nature of the international calendar and it's something I know we both had to get used to and are still getting used to … I said a few times that it's almost like we are grandparents. We get to see the players for a week or so and then we send them back to their parents, which is their clubs."

Outside of her tactical expertise, though, Hayes represents U.S. Soccer's ambitious turn in recent years as much as Pochettino does. She was hired because of her reputation as a serial winner at Chelsea, where she won eight league titles and seven cups. She continued the trend in short order with the USWNT – two months after officially starting in the role, she won Olympic gold at the Paris Games in 2024. U.S. Soccer has equally ambitious goals for the men's team, though the timeline will understandably be longer for that program. They continue to target the USMNT's first World Cup quarterfinal appearance since 2002 but in between, they also hope to medal in the Olympics' men's soccer event, which is contested by U-23 teams, for the first time when the Games come to Los Angeles in 2028. More than many at the federation, Hayes has experience with the intangibles it takes to reach those heights and that's exactly why she was hired in the first place. It also reflects what U.S. Soccer's executives are looking for in the next USMNT head coach.

"The most important characteristic is someone with ambition that matches ours, which is high and so when you have, then, that high shared ambition, then you look for the experience, the talent, the understanding that accompanies that ambition," Helfrich said.

Beyond that, though, Hayes in particular has an idea of what the USMNT job might entail. She is the best of both worlds – she began her coaching career in the U.S. two decades ago and has a deep understanding of the American soccer landscape, but made a name for herself in her native England and can also bring a useful outsider's perspective. There is no perfect equivalent to Hayes waiting for the USMNT job since no coach with experience in the American game has truly broken into the top tiers of the sport just yet, the federation likely to settle for one or the other. Hayes' understanding of both orbits, though, makes her an important guiding force along the way. She might be the only qualified person to answer how much to weigh the insider's perspective with the accomplished outsider's point of view when looking for the next USMNT head coach, in large part because she is the only person who boasts an equal share of it.

Hayes' expertise alone means she will be as valuable a sounding board as any, to the point that it's hard to minimize her ability to offer input down to one or two straightforward things. There is one more thing Hayes might have that no one at U.S. Soccer does – easy access to some of the most notable coaches in the game.

Over the course of her successful 12-year tenure at Chelsea, Hayes became one of the most respected coaches in England. She became the first woman to win the Football Writers Association's Tribute Award in 2024 shortly before leaving England for the U.S., and has earned the praise of many of her counterparts in the men's game along the way. Out of anyone at U.S. Soccer, Hayes might actually have the most compelling list of phone numbers in her contacts. She has said Sir Alex Ferguson, a coaching legend if there ever was one after his storied 27-year tenure at Manchester United, calls her "from time to time." Hayes has been in touch with a handful of her contemporaries over the years, including those who have been on U.S. Soccer's radar at one point or another. In her 2024 book, "A Completely Different Game," Hayes said she heard from Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp after having an emergency hysterectomy because of endometriosis in 2022. The pair "sent me long messages, expressing deeply felt emotions," as did Graham Potter and David Moyes.

The rolodex is a covetable one, if ex-U.S. Soccer sporting director Matt Crocker can serve as an example. His greatest accomplishments during his three-year spell, which came to an end in April when he took a similar role with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation, were hiring Hayes and Pochettino. He had previously worked with Pochettino at Southampton a decade earlier, which made U.S. Soccer's approach easier when discussions started. Hayes' value exceeds her ability to hand her bosses a phone number but it is unlikely to go unnoticed at U.S. Soccer, who clearly understands the expertise she would bring to the search in a variety of ways.

#1186. NWSL announces new player development rule to incentivize youth investment, aims for further expansion

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest week on the NWSL calendar is here as the buildup towards the 2026 NWSL Championship is underway. An awards show, countless events, and media days were all on the agenda ahead of Saturday's big game. That included the annual state of the league by commissioner Jessica Berman on Thursday.

This year, the commissioner welcomed media to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., and celebrated record ticket sales, attendance, and future expansion ahead of Saturday night's championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current, live on CBS at 8 p.m. ET. She also announced a few new league rules and future match events.

The commissioner introduced the new player development rule. While the league previously submitted paperwork for a potential future second=division league, conversation and planning around that is currently paused with the upcoming 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and efforts to grow NWSL in other ways.

"As we grow from 16 to 18 teams in 2028, we know that we have to prioritize the pipeline, not just the pipeline of players, but the pipeline of talent that supports the players in the daily training environment. One of the things that makes the United States so uniquely positioned in the global women's soccer landscape is the depth of that potential pipeline," said Berman in her opening remarks.

"That's why today we're announcing the NWSL Player Development Rule. It's an important step in strengthening the pathway to professional soccer for the next generation of players. The rule creates actual incentives for clubs to invest in identifying, developing, and retaining young talent, and it gives the clubs the flexibility to design their programs in the way that makes sense with their sporting philosophies."

More information and the types of incentives will roll out for clubs as the new player development rule goes into effect, but it is another step in future roster-building for clubs now alongside general player signings, transfers, the High Impact Player rule, and the Under-18 mechanism.

The addition of the rule is paving the way for more support staff and systems in place. The commissioner also announced the new NWSL Sporting Executive Program, meant to provide more support for club leadership development. The inaugural set of leadership includes six executives from the league who will participate in the program.

"Developing the future of the sport is not just limited to the players; it's also about the technical staff who surround those players each and every day ... this is a first-of-its-kind program invested in talent, and it was curated and developed in collaboration with U.S. Soccer and FIFA. This new year-long initiative will provide sporting executives at our clubs with curated, specialized education, mentorship, and leadership development opportunities tailored around the unique demands of our league and the women's professional game," she said.

The NWSL commissioner then announced the future site of the next NWSL Challenge Cup. The 2027 NWSL Challenge Cup will take place in Austin, Texas, next summer.

The tournament has evolved since its first iteration as a placeholder for the COVID-19-affected season and is now a unique one-off marquee match between top clubs, typically the NWSL Shield titleholders and the NWSL Championship winners. In years where one club wins both, the game is a rematch of the previous NWSL Championship match.

"Following the success of this year's Challenge Cup in Columbus, where we took the event to a neutral site to give an opportunity to introduce the NWSL to a new community," she said.

The 2026 NWSL Challenge Cup was between 2025 NWSL Shield winners Kansas City Current and 2025 NWSL Championship winners Gotham FC. The 2026 competition was held in Columbus, Ohio. The state will now welcome its first NWSL franchise in 2028 alongside another expansion club in Atlanta.

Fans will undoubtedly make the connection and wonder if there is a future where an NWSL club calls Austin home. Currently, there are three NWSL clubs in California and only one in Texas, the Houston Dash.

"We're really excited to create another special experience for our fans and our players while making the NWSL a place that can invite new audiences," Berman said about heading to Austin.

Commissioner Berman celebrated the league's recent return to the nation's capital for another NWSL Championship. The city hosted the 2022 event and now returns four years later with more attention on the league, the clubs, and its players than ever before.

"Today, we're bigger, stronger, more visible, and more ambitious than ever before, and the next five years are going to redefine what's possible. We have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us, and we intend to seize it," she said.

Two incoming clubs set for 2028 and new player roster rules are just the beginning of NWSL's next chapter. There's still the potential for more clubs on the horizon, and current clubs Houston Dash and Racing Louisville are in the process of vetting for a sale to new ownership as franchise entry fees into the league are booming to new heights.

And of course, there is still the biggest game of the year to play on Saturday.

"The Washington Spirit are back in the championship for the third consecutive year, determined to bring home that title. And standing in their way is the Kansas City Current, with its own ambitions to win a championship after winning the Shield in 2025. These are two exceptional clubs, two incredibly passionate fan base, and the championship is still to be decided, [we're] very excited about the rest of this week."

#1185. Xabi Alonso hits back at former Liverpool team-mate Jamie Carragher's scathing criticism of his Chelsea centre-backs Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana

Published: 03:35 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 03:35 EST, 27 November 2026

Xabi Alonso concedes Chelsea's defending has been nowhere near good enough – but the Blues boss believes his friend Jamie Carragher was wrong to brand Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana a 'massive problem' in his scathing analysis of the centre-back pairing.

Alonso claimed he had not seen Carragher's critique on Sky Sports' Monday Night Football after their 4-1 home loss to Leeds United.

When told his former Liverpool team-mate had said Colwill and Fofana 'will never work' as defensive partners and that Chelsea 'will never achieve anything' without fixing this problem, Alonso said: 'I must disagree. I disagree with Carra.

'For sure, you can have bad games. We were not good. But I've seen them play well, and I've seen them show good levels.

'This is the goal and the challenge – to be consistent in the performance and to be consistent in the basics and not to drop in certain games when we are facing a tough opponent. I understand it was not good enough.'

Colwill and Fofana were bullied by Dominic Calvert-Lewin of Leeds, as they also were by Sunderland's Brian Brobbey. They will now face Liam Delap and Nottingham Forest on Friday night at a City Ground which will carry an intimidating atmosphere.

Xabi Alonso has hit back at former Liverpool team-mate Jamie Carragher after he labelled Chelsea's centre backs a massive problem

Alonso and Carragher spent five seasons together as team-mates at Liverpool

Alonso was strong in saying his side can have 'no excuses' for their slipping standards, having conceded 20 Premier League goals this season. 'When you have that feeling like we had on Saturday, it is not good,' the Chelsea manager said.

'We have talked about what we can do better and what we have to do better. There are no excuses not to do better. There are things that we all can do, even if you have a bad day in terms of feeling something you have to do at this level.

'The feeling of the last game is not good, but now it's about looking forward and showing a reaction. There are no excuses. There is no ifs, no buts. Just certainties and things we have to do.

'We can define on the training and the messaging. We need to show that, not just talk. Talk is cheap. It's about performing on the pitch.'

John Terry works for Chelsea's academy part-time, assisting the youngsters coming through at Cobham. Terry is a club legend whose two strengths were defending and leadership.

Asked if he had thought about bringing him on to his staff, Alonso said: 'We have talked because he's been around Cobham many times.

'He's working with the academy. We have people in the staff to prepare for that, and, for sure, the presence of John is always welcome.'

Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana have endured poor starts to the season with Chelsea having already conceded 20 Premier League goals

Pressed further on whether he had worked with the first team, Alonso added: 'This year? Not yet. But he's close to the team.'

Meanwhile, Fofana has apologised to Chelsea for the unauthorised interview he conducted with a YouTuber which sparked a backlash from supporters online.

In it, the centre-back laughed off his penalty miss which condemned the club to their Carabao Cup exit at Liverpool, and revealed how his representatives advised him to honour his lucrative contract, worth £200,000 per week, when he was tempted to quit football amid his injury hell.

Alonso confirmed the club had spoken with Fofana and said: 'He apologised. He knows it was not right, the moment, and it was not right, the content. We are here to take things seriously and he said that it's not going to be repeated.'

When asked if Fofana had been fined, Alonso said: 'This is internal things.'
