#1143. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

A fantastic pass from Gyökeres and a lovely finish from Madueke 🪄 The Arsenal attackers combine to great effect 🤝 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/blmMILZxok

Just as Gyokeres is finding his form, so is Madueke. The absence of the injured Bukayo Saka has given Madueke a run in the side and he seems to be benefiting from it, even if he still lacks the same consistency in decision-making as his England team-mate.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Merino were all alternating positions at will, taking turns to drop deep and push forward. Merino could have scored a couple, before he combined sharply with Gyokeres for Arsenal’s second.

Gyokeres has never been the most delicate link-up player, and there have been too many times when the ball has simply bounced off him, but here he was impressively sleek. A quick exchange of passes with Merino allowed him a sight of goal, and the curled finish was sumptuous. For a man known for his power, this was an uncharacteristic demonstration of finesse.

Game over? Arsenal clearly thought so. They certainly came out for the second half like a team that believed the job was done. Arteta became increasingly irate in the first few minutes after the restart, with Ben White on the receiving end of one verbal slap. Rice also received a telling-off, and a yellow card, from the referee after kicking the ball away in annoyance.

Would Slavia have secured a draw if they had been at full strength? They had been weakened by the banishment of their star striker from the club because of a series of disciplinary failings. Tomás Chory, the top scorer for the past two seasons, was chucked out of the team after showing his middle finger to the referee in a recent game. This sort of sanction would have earned Arteta’s approval, no doubt, but it did not increase Slavia’s chances of hurting the Premier League champions in those edgy final few minutes.

Perhaps they will reflect on that decision differently now, given the uncharacteristically wobbly second-half performance by Arsenal. The visitors were vulnerable in the latter stages, when they lacked the control and composure that Arteta expects. Gabriel, too, appeared dismayed by what he was seeing. At one point, he put his hands on his hips and scowled at his team-mates like an angry teacher.

With only a few minutes remaining, Nowak converted a left-wing cross to plunge Arsenal into a proper panic. It required a backs-to-the-wall defensive action, similar to the victory against Liverpool on Sunday, to get over the line.

Always we need to value winning away in the Champions League. It is extremely difficult. Two very different halves. We should have had three or four goals in the first half but we didn’t do it. Right at the start of the second half we were on the back foot, very sloppy and gave balls away. Then we had to suffer. A lot to learn.

We should have scored more in the first half and if we didn’t do that we had to go and do that in the second half.

We made six changes but we know the quality of the players we have. Whether we were lacking something I don’t know but I would have done the same thing [again].

I value what the team has done now, it is 11 away games we played, but our standards should be higher.

Arteta on Gyokeres: "He was really good. A game we believed was good for him, for the spaces he could use. He was really connected to the team. Great news because I think he needed that. Really pleased."

Arteta: "Two very different halves. The first we played at a really high level. At half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning we were extremely far from our standards. Very far from the standards we expect from each other."

First half we played really, really well. We created a lot of chances and could have scored more but the second half was completely different. They stepped up a gear and made it difficult for us and we have to learn from it. Delighted with the win but a lot of things to improve going forward.

Maybe they started pressing a bit higher with more intensity. We had too many giveaways especially in the final third. There was too much running from box to box and we have to manage those reactions and go for the third and fourth goal.

At the end of the day it is three points.

Slavia Prague managed just one shot on goal in the first half worth 0.12 xG but finished the game with 18 shots on Arsenal’s goal and 2.23 xG. Arsenal could easily have dropped points on the balance of the second 45 minutes.

Quite surprised Declan Rice stayed on the pitch for the full 90 minutes there. He seemed to be in a bit of discomfort after a couple of long sprints. And then he got the silly yellow. Arteta perhaps panicking about the result.

🚨 𝐎𝐅𝐅𝐈𝐂𝐈𝐀𝐋: Viktor Gyökeres has been named Player of the Match vs. Slavia Prague. ⭐️🇸🇪 https://t.co/mtzVKvNlpq

A top-two finish means home second legs all the way, and avoidance of the league phase winners until the final.

Arsenal put another win on the board in the Champions League, but what looked like being a cakewalk at half-time was anything but. Arteta will use that second 45 minutes to demonstrate the dangers of not starting a half with full intensity, once Slavia were in top it was hard to wrestle back control.

Arsenal were second best in midfield, it was strange that Lewis-Skelly and Guimaraes stayed on the bench, but they stumbled over the line.

Arsenal have a throw-in deep in Slavia Prague territory, but a Rice foul gives the home team one last chance to launch the ball forward. The goalkeeper goes long, but Arsenal send it backwards.

Only for a while though, but Konecny’s shot was tame and straight at Raya.

Glancing header loops over the Arsenal bar, Sadilek’s cross dangerous again.

Then Max Dowman wins a free-kick in midfield with a neat piece of control.

Another ball flashes across the Arsenal box but they survive. Then Madueke wins a free-kick in the Slavia Prague half. Three minutes to play. And Max Dowman is coming on to replace Madueke.

Nowak is the player who has scored it, but it was created by a wonderful left-footed cross from Jurasek, which split Raya and the Arsenal defenders. It could be a nervy finish now.

But hold on... VAR is checking for offside. Goal given!

Slavia Praha pull one back late on ⏱️ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/N0qYWAlKHa

Arsenal have another corner to defend after Kubiak’s shot deflects behind. Declan Rice heads away at the near post.

Arsenal enjoying more possession now in the Slavia Prague half, Odegaard helping in that regard. They have knocked off since half-time in truth, Slavia have not quite had the quality to punish them.

If Arsenal had more pace to offer from the bench, there might be a third goal in this.

Odegaard and Tzolis have shots blocked, before Raya makes a magnificent save to keep out Kubiak’s header at the other end. The Slavia Prague player leapt in front of Timber, but Raya tipped the ball on to the post before keeping the ball in front of the line.

Slavia Prague swing in another dangerous cross but they fail to make the post of it. They have been the dominant force since half-time, but the damage was done in the first 45 minutes.

Arsenal starting to live a little dangerously: Hincapie misses his kick in his own penalty area, and Zima shoots over the bar.

Arteta has seen enough and is making a double sub: Gyokeres and White off, Timber and Odegaard on.

Raya gets himself in some trouble from the corner but Gabriel heads off the goal-line! Then there was a clash of heads between Merino and a Slavia player... and VAR is checking for a penalty.

Eventually, the right decision is reached: it was a clash of heads in a 50:50.

Slavia Prague have a corner that Gabriel was forced to give away. Merino did well to head clear, and then Jurasek’s strike from distance deflects behind for another corner.

Probably the closest Arsenal have come to a third goal, with Madueke rifling a shot at the goalkeeper from a tight angle. Then there was an Arsenal break lead by Rice, but he ran out of puff at the edge of the box. Slavia Prague players are going to ground very easily looking for free-kicks.

Declan Rice has now been booked for a hand in the face of Sadilek, or possibly for kicking the ball away after the referee blew his whistle. Slavia Prague continue to ask questions, but David Raya has not been stretched.

Mosquera with a strong recovery run to defend against Ayaosi in the corner at the expense of a throw-in. It feels like Arsenal are through their rough patch at the start of the half, but Arteta will want the third.

Here come some Arsenal changes: Mosquera on for Konsa (who has been booked), and Tzolis on for Eze.

Slavia’s man-to-man pressing has been far more suffocating in this half, but there was a reminder there that when Arsenal get it right there is space to attack. Raya almost sold Rice short, but he whipped a ball around the corner first time to Merino, who played forward. Still no Arsenal changes.

Slavia Prague enjoying a period of possession but it is all in front of Arsenal.

Then Madueke loses the ball in a promising position, and Ayaosi is running right at the Arsenal back four. Konsa partially blocks his shot, but it deflects behind for a corner. Good delivery over Raya, but it bounces out for a goal kick.

Konsa with a storming run forward and a floated cross as Arsenal come alive as an attacking force, but it breaks down with a Ben White foul on the edge of the box.

Ezri Konsa booked after Ayaosi gets to a loose ball first near the touchline. Moments before that, White and Raya messed about with the ball and there were some choice words from Rice and Arteta. Arsenal have dropped their standards so far in the half.

Arteta is really raging on the touchline. He is not happy with how Arsenal have started this second half. He just aimed a few verbals at White for a defensive mix-up. White had actually already received an apology from Raya and didn’t seem to think it was his fault.

Rice with a chance to pick out Madueke on the counter but his diagonal pass was cut out. Slavia have been sent out with a flea in their ear, and have been much improved so far. Arteta will want Arsenal to stay serious and weather this spell.

Tonight has been a reminder of how good Martin Zubimendi is in the air. He’s wearing a face mask because of a broken nose but he’s won every header he has gone for. He’s not particularly tall but he has a great leap and timing.

Slavia Prague have a free-kick on the edge of Arsenal’s box after Konsa goes sliding in. Much more like it from Slavia Prague early on, Arsenal a little dozy since the restart.

Kubiak shoots low from the free-kick, but it is straight into the wall.

The home crowd have something to shout about for the first time tonight. Kubiak brings a decent save out of David Raya after shooting with his left foot from 25 yards. Then Raya slices a kick out for a throw-in.

Slavia have made a double sub: Suleiman and Sturm off, N’Guessan and Chytil on.

From the early stages of the game, the home team have tried to sprint up to the ball and pressure Arsenal, but they have been manipulated and played through so easily at times. When they do lock on man-to-man, Arsenal are hitting Madueke, Eze and Gyokeres early who are pinning defenders and then laying the ball off to runners.

Arsenal are dispatching another Champions League league phase opponent with ease, but the big positive has been the performances of Eze, Gyokeres and Madueke. Without Saka, Arteta needs them to step up and provide goals and assists. Albeit against poor opposition, they have all looked dangerous. Might we see half-time changes with Saturday’s game against Hull in mind?

Kubiak down and there are loud appeals for a Slavia free-kick but the referee was not having any of it. Gyokeres proves an otlet again, but his pass towards Madueke was too strong.

Arsenal have a corner and they are rampant. Eze with a flick around the corner which almost finds Gyokeres, they are playing with plenty of attacking panache. The quality of opposition needs accounting for but Arteta will be delighted given he made six changes.

Gabriel then threatens after Domchak spills Madueke’s cross, but his effort was blocked.

Arsenal wasted a counter initially with Eze running into a Zubimendi pass but they kept it alive and eventually punished their hosts. Merino with a cute pass back into Gyokeres’s path, and he took his time before curling a shot in off the far post. Arsenal should not be caught from here.

If you thought the Gyokeres assist was good, then that goal was even better. Gorgeous finish. That takes him to three assists and two goals in his past five games.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

Slavia Prague have had their first shot: Holes poking wide after a long throw was hurled into the box. Not much more than a half chance.

The referee is now having a word with Rice after he complained about Eze not being awarded a free-kick. Slavia have settled down a touch after that very rocky period, but they are still to muster a shot on goal.

Declan Rice is throwing a blanket over any flickering embers of a Slavia Prague attack, and then he is running the game from there. Arsenal’s captain on the night has been imperious so far.

Now Declan Rice feeds the ball straight through the six-yard box but Hincapie could not quite make it his to score a tap-in. Surely a question of when not if Arsenal put this game to bed.

Eze and Madueke are feeling it tonight. Slavia’s full-backs have been going through footballing hell in this opening half an hour.

Eze and Hincapie’s turn to cause problems down the left, the left-back’s pull-back evaded everyone, before Eze sat down the defender in the box but his shot was blocked.

Then Domchak saves from point-blank range to deny Merino! Slick play between Madueke and White to carve out the chance.

Arsenal really should have buried the second.

Domchak claimed Rice’s cross from the free-kick and Slavia Prague tried to counter-attack, but it was really diligent defensive work from Madueke to snuff out the danger. Arsenal continue to look in complete control.

Madueke then proves a thorn in the Slavia defence’s side, sitting down the left-back and standing up a cross to the back post. Gyokeres won the header, then Merino glanced over.

A moment of promise from Slavia Prague, but their pull-back to the edge of the box is picked up by Arsenal and Eze skips through a couple of challenges before being brought down by Moses. Yellow card for the Slavia Prague midfielder.

Then Ayaosi concedes a cheap free-kick against Hincapie, in a crossing position wide left.

Arsenal leaving themselves light at the back, but White, Gabriel and Konsa are happy dealing with the one-on-one duels, they look physically stronger than the Slavia forwards. Madueke, aside from his goal, has been very tidy on the ball so far.

Sharp interplay from Gyokeres and Eze again, teeing up Merino to sting the palms of the goalkeeper with a shot from the edge of the box. Arsenal corner.

Last time out in the Champions League against Lille, Arsenal’s squad players in attack failed to seize their chance but this has been much more promising from them.

Domchak makes a scrambling save on the line to stop Arsenal going two up, and possibly killing the game. Zubimendi’s break forward created the danger, and Gyokeres and Hincapie were close to applying the finish.

There was a moment just after scoring where Hincapie was caught forward on the overlap, and who else but Declan Rice was on hand to mop up the counter-attack in the left-back zone? Order restored, and Arsenal back on top in the game soon after.

Slavia Prague make a mess of a simple long ball forward, disobeying the old maxim that says never let the ball bounce. Gyokeres was alive though, hooking the ball behind the defence with a clever early pass. Madueke’s pace was always going to send him clear, and he slipped the ball through the legs of the goalkeeper Domchak.

That didn’t take long. Arsenal have dominated the ball in these opening exchanges and now they have scored with their first real chance. It’s a lovely pass by Gyokeres, who is not known for his intricate build-up play, and Madueke’s pace gets him behind. Madueke’s third goal of the season.

A fantastic pass from Gyökeres and a lovely finish from Madueke 🪄 The Arsenal attackers combine to great effect 🤝 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/blmMILZxok

With Merino, Zubimendi and Rice in Arsenal’s midfield, there is perhaps no natural creator, but the three of them are rotating, taking it in turns to stand between the centre-backs or go high.

Madueke stands up a cross which Slavia Prague head clear. Most of the game is being played in the home team’s half, which you would expect. Arsenal probing and moving the ball patiently.

Madueke and Ben White then combine well, but Eze cannot quite let fly from a central position. The Arsenal left-winger drifting across the line to receive the ball in that move.

Quite an industrious start from the home team, trying to close Arsenal down, but Merino and Zubimendi combined well in a tight space to help Arsenal move forward. The flag goes up against Ben White for offside, possibly mistakenly.

At the other end Sturm caused Konsa a problem, but the Arsenal defender recovered well and the goal kick decision was in his favour too, much to the annoyance of the home crowd.

Arsenal also paid their respects at Colney to the 30-year-old Spanish player who died after a collision with the Andorra’s goalkeeper.

Declan Rice is wearing the captain’s armband and leads Arsenal out at a smoky Fortuna Arena. Slavia Prague are celebrating their 144th birthday, and marked the occasion with a choir and classical music.

William Saliba is BACK 💥 https://t.co/aRmJoIlxSc

Liverpool twice threw away a lead to lose against Fenerbahce in Istanbul. That has some relevance to Arsenal because Liverpool are one of the teams above them in the league phase table. Win in Prague, and they will move one point clear of their Premier League rivals.

Real Madrid struck late to drag themselves out of jail at AEK Athens and join PSG on maximum points from four games. Arsenal cannot catch those two sides tonight, but they do host Real next month.

Slavia are without their top scorer from the last two seasons, Tomas Chory, for rather unusual reasons. He has been banished from the club following a series of misdemeanours, the latest of which was showing the middle finger to the referee in a recent league game. Slavia have made it clear he won’t be playing for the club again, despite his importance to the team over the past few years.

Chory was also sent off for Czech Republic against Turkey at Euro 2024.

😬 Pandemonium after the final whistle! Czech Republic's Tomáš Chorý is shown a red card, with multiple others yellow carded, as players and staff from both sides clash 🟥 #Euro2024 | #CZETUR https://t.co/5xhR0Bwafa

Without meaning to be rude, I think it’s fair to say Slavia are not the most formidable opponent that Arsenal will face this season.

They are on a 22-game winless streak in the Champions League, dating back to 2007. If they don’t win tonight, they will equal the longest winless run in European Cup/Champions League history, shared with AEK Athens (1989-2006) and Steau Bucharest (2006-2013).

Slavia Prague XI: Domchak, Holes, Zima, Vlcek, Suleiman, Moses, Sadilek, Kubiak, Ayaosi, Sturm, Nowak

Subs: Markovic, Rezek, Chaloupek, N’Guessan, Chytil, Provod, Diakite, Kacor, Jurasek, Konecny, Barcot, Kotrba

Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

On that occasion last year, Max Dowman became the youngest player in Champions League history. He should get more minutes tonight from the bench, given that he is currently suspended from Premier League action following his controversial red card against Fleetwood last week.

That’s the most Arteta has rotated between a Premier League and Champions League game so far this season. Telling perhaps that Konsa, Gabriel and Rice – the team’s defensive bedrock – stay in place. But changes on both sides at full-back, and in the attacking midfield areas.

Arsenal XI: Raya; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Zubimendi, Merino; Madueke, Gyokeres, Eze

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, Saliba, Mosquera, Timber, Calafiori, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard, Guimaraes, Tzolis, Dowman, Havertz

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Six changes for our Champions League test 👊

Arsenal’s critics will still grumble about the style of victory, but, of all clubs, this is a team who have no obligation to play in a way that neutrals might enjoy. Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Now they are mostly effective but only occasionally stylish on such occasions. If you asked all the travelling fans at Anfield which they prefer, you would receive an overwhelming response.

David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 54% of his Champions League starts (21 clean sheets from 39 starts), the best ratio of any goalkeeper to start at least 25 games in the competition. 🤯🇪🇸 https://t.co/A1Zpn8kJN9

Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#1142. Revealed: The numbers that show Man United are NOT too good to go down - they have the worst defence in Europe, are constantly outrun by opponents and are one of the most wasteful teams in the Premier League

Published: 09:45 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:03 EST, 27 November 2026

Manchester United are not too good to go down and absolutely are in a relegation battle. They aren’t good, let’s start there.

Getting heavily beaten away to Liverpool was not at all surprising to Manchester United fans. If anything, many feared an even heavier scoreline.

Not since 1973-74 have Manchester United been relegated and on that occasion that rag-tag group had won three of its first 11 matches. This time around, the side Mauricio Pochettino has inherited has just one win to its name.

Former players and pundits believe that eventually, yes, United will get their act together and that relegation isn’t really something to be preoccupied with right now. Fools gold.

Chief executive Omar Berrada claimed with a straight face that the club is heading in the right direction only last week. As staggering a statement last Friday as it was by the time the final whistle sounded on Sunday. By that point, it was insulting.

Slumped in 19th and it will be 90 days since their last league win by the time they host Brentford at Old Trafford in a bid to stop the rot on Saturday, United’s problems are threatening to engulf Pochettino and his staff - even though they showed positive signs in the battling draw in Lisbon on Wednesday.

Daily Mail Sport takes a look at the stats that condemn this sorry United squad and why burying their heads in the hand at talk of a relegation battle is the last thing they can afford to do…

Manchester United are not too good to go down and absolutely are in a relegation battle

Trust Manchester United to be top of the table for the very worst statistic, officially having the worst defence in Europe’s top five leagues.

Luis Suarez's late goal for Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday made it 36 goals conceded in total by United across all competitions, taking them ahead of Lens (35), Crystal Palace (34), Getafe (34) and Union Berlin (33).

That’s a Lens side that conceded nine in one match in the Champions League. That’s an Union Berlin side who has conceded five or more goals three times already this campaign, including a 7-0 drubbing at the hands of Bayern Munich.

Individually and collectively United lack any sort of structure, any sort of desire to do the basics, any sort of solidity that will have opposition forwards thinking twice.

Open it up to the top four leagues in England and United are one of only two teams yet to manage a single league clean sheet this season, with fellow Premier League outfit Ipswich Town. League Two side Barnet was on that list until they kept their first clean sheet of the season against Crawley on Tuesday.

Specifically in the Premier League, United rank 19th for Big Chances Against (22.2), rank 19th for Expected Goals Against (xGA). They have the sixth-worst Expected Goals differential in the league.

The Red Devils have the worst defence in Europe’s top five leagues, conceding 36 goals so far

Matthijs de Ligt looked all at sea in his first league start in 357 days away to Liverpool to the point whereby Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher said they ‘felt sorry’ for him. Leny Yoro continues to make costly mistakes. Diogo Dalot no longer looks up to the level. Noussair Mazraoui has regressed massively. Patrick Dorgu looks uncomfortable defending. Harry Maguire lacks recovery pace to go toe-to-toe with top defenders. Ayden Heaven is raw. Lisandro Martinez is a shadow of the best version previously seen at United. And Luke Shaw is injured.

It a defence that is majorly short on quality, discipline and leadership and that’s underscored by the amount of times they concede in bunches.

United shipped two goals in eight minutes away to Como and conceded two in five minutes a few days later against Bournemouth.

Twice in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa they conceded in bunches with two first half goals in three minutes, followed up by two Villa goals in five minutes in the second.

Add in the two goals in six minutes at home against Roma – a game where the attack bailed out the defence in a 3-2 win – and the two goals shipped at Anfield in three minutes against Liverpool, this United rearguard is not fit for purpose.

Put these defenders in a neutral kit and unanimously they’d be seen as relegation candidates.

Mauricio Pochettino must sort out Manchester United's leaky defence as a top priority

That’s what set pieces are to United, a complete disaster.

Poor sides in the Premier League often must hang their hats on scoring timely goals and grinding out vital wins through the means of set-pieces.

United do not look capable of doing that.

In the Premier League, they are joint-20th for set-piece goals conceded so far this season with seven, while they rank 19th for set-piece goals scored (1). Only Nottingham Forest (0) are performing worse in this area than United.

Set-piece xG places United 19th in the league with 2.6, only marginally ahead of Gary O’Neil’s Ipswich Town, who are 20th with a set-piece xG of 1.6.

Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic hinted after the opening weekend’s 2-0 win over United that the Red Devils are easy to prepare for when it comes to set pieces, the area which created both goals.

Last season United ranked second, only behind champions Arsenal, for set-piece goals scored and 11th for set-piece goals conceded.

Pochettino took issue with Chelsea’s hierarchy when they went over his head to appoint a dedicated set-piece coach and there is no suggestion one such guru is heading United’s way.

But make no bones about it, United have regressed massively in this area and it’s a slide without an easy fix.

Luis Suarez capitalises on Senne Lammens' error to equalise for Sporting Lisbon late on

One of the biggest concerns right now is the ease at which teams are cutting United open.

Bournemouth are a very good team but their win at Old Trafford looked like a training game at times.

Against Villa, John McGinn strolled through the game, even if they went on to draw 4-4. There are too many examples of this.

At 111.5km on average per game, United rank 19th in the league for distance covered per match, with only Sunday’s victors Liverpool clocking in further ground coverage.

Worse than that, United badly lack pace and athleticism in the middle of the park as well as in wide areas. Where Liverpool fans marvel at the likes of Rio Ngumoha and Bradley Barcola, United have built a squad severely lacking pace in all areas.

Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha are better inside and lack blistering pace. Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw have both been exposed defensively for pace this season. Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are technically very good operators but both lack athleticism and are therefore losing the midfield battle too often.

Pochettino’s predecessor Michael Carrick scoffed at the fixation on running stats before he was sacked and there is some merit to it not being the be-all-and-end-all – look at Liverpool.

But only Aston Villa (10) have been outrun by opponents more through the opening 11 games than United (9) and that, factored in with a porous defence and a soft underbelly at set pieces has United out there like a lamb for slaughter a lot of the time.

The appointment of Sam Wilson as first-team fitness coach, a move agreed long in advance of Pochettino’s hiring, from Arsenal will look to address the serious levels of underperformance in this area.

But with so little time on the training pitch and free moments in the schedule to fix months of fitness regression, it’s a gargantuan task.

Man United badly lack pace and athleticism in the middle of the park as well as in wide areas

As Pochettino had his head in his hands at Anfield he’d have been forgiven for wondering just how he was actually going to stop this sinking ship from fully going under.

He was back at Carrington at 6:30am on Monday morning staring at a schedule that promises 10 games in 39 days.

Players were back in for recovery sessions on Monday and training on Tuesday ahead of flying to Lisbon to face Sporting on Wednesday. Despite picking up a first point under Pochettino, there were plenty of individual errors in the 2-2 draw, namely with Senne Lammens conceding a needless penalty and later gifting Sporting an equaliser after failing to gather the ball in the air.

With recovery on Thursday, it means there is only time for a light Friday session pre-Brentford on Saturday, when it will have been 90 days since United’s last league win.

For all of the reasons outlined above, United are like a boxer on the ropes that is just trying to hang in there for the remainder of the year as the blows keep raining down.

There are problems aplenty in defence and athleticism is one of the biggest worries. But mentality and belief is what Pochettino and his staff need to inspire as soon as possible.

With a busy schedule of games, Pochettino and his coaching team don't have time on their side

United are the only team in the Premier League not to win a single game across the last seven, while they are one of only two teams in the 92 in the Football League to have just one domestic win this season, along with Burnley.

Having fallen behind eight times in the league, United have gone on to win just once, beating Ipswich Town. That was the anomaly.

From winning positions, they rank 19th for points won, taking just six points from the four games in which they held the lead.

And, ultimately, what are United’s players and fans clinging to?

They rank 17th for home form and 19th away from home, where they have scored just four goals, while they are 18th in the league for shot conversion (5%) having taken the most shots (280) in the league. Only Sunderland and Nottingham Forest are more wasteful.

United still have to travel to Newcastle United and Arsenal before the year is out, both daunting trips for sides low on confidence, while Champions League hopes hang in the balance against Sporting and RB Leipzig.

Pochettino has a list as long as his arm with what he needs to fix but he has to get players believing again. It’s November and things are bad now, but they cannot throw in the towel when the going gets tough.

At this stage, indications are that the budget to be afforded to Pochettino in January will be ‘modest’ and is not set to be the splurge United likely need it to be.

Calvin Bassey and Nathan Collins are on a list of targets, while Jarrad Branthwaite has been admired for a long time, albeit would be a player who would prove very expensive to get out of Everton mid-season.

United need to add at least two high-quality defenders in January, if not three, to give them a chance of salvaging a season that is threatening to get away from them.

The likes of Maguire, De Ligt, Dalot and Mazraoui are not suddenly going to improve and while there is a belief among former players that they won’t go down and it’s not a conversation to be had, those upstairs, who have failed miserably to date, cannot afford to show the same level of flippancy in what is set to be the most critical transfer window in decades for United.

Get it wrong and they could run out of road come May.

Indications are that the budget to be afforded to Pochettino by Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left) and Omar Berrada (right) in January will be ‘modest’, despite Manchester United needing reinforcements

It raised alarm last Sunday night when it was pointed out that Tottenham Hotspur, who finished 17th and survived by the skin of their teeth last season, had 18 points after 11 games last season, 10 points more than United currently have.

In fact, since 2019-20, 20 different teams have had eight or fewer points after 11 Premier League games and 14 have gone down.

Two seasons ago both Crystal Palace and Wolverhampton Wanderers sat with fewer points than United after 11 games and both survived comfortably.

But the general trend is those there now will be there when all is said and done.

#1141. Champions League expert picks, predictions, best bets: Will Arsenal overcome absent David Raya vs. Dortmund?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Matchday 5 is here, and the Champions League league phase's second half means four games are left to lock in spots in the knockouts. Just four games in, there's still room to do enough to advance or enough time to come up short. Drop a couple more points and that top-eight bye turns into two more games in the playoff round for teams like Liverpool and Manchester City who are just inside the top eight. For sides such as Manchester United, Bayern Munich and Inter, finding their footing will be incredibly vital if they dream of advancing as part of that top eight. Tuesday's slate sees Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund at the Emirates, Manchester City welcome Napoli and Real Madrid take on PSV Eindhoven.

Wednesday is when things may get even more wild, with numerous teams on upset watch, with many eyes on Mauricio Pochettino's Man United after their ugly 4-0 loss at Liverpool over the weekend. Leny Yoro's early red card essentially confirmed defeat for a team that has regularly failed to compete with 11 men, let alone 10. Will they put things together this week against Sporting?

Here are our expert picks for this matchday:

Every match streams live on Paramount+, your home for every Champions League game all season long, plus replays, highlights, and studio coverage breaking down the race for the top eight.

Player to watch: Kepa Arrizabalaga, Arsenal -- Mikel Arteta soothed fears of the worst possible outcome after David Raya's injury at Newcastle on Saturday evening, but there can be no doubt that the biggest drop-off between starter and reserve in the Arsenal squad is between the posts. Kepa's spell in the XI may be brief; can the Gunners get through it unscathed? -- James BengeMan of the match: Christos Tzolis, Arsenal -- There is no doubt this is the kind of game he needs to shine, as Arteta needs to make some rotations in his team. Tzolis has been a great addition to the roster, but he's yet to score his first goal of the season, despite having assisted his teammates twice so far in both Champions League and Premier League games. -- Francesco Porzio

Prediction: Arsenal 2, Borussia Dortmund 0 -- Borussia Dortmund have done well in the Bundesliga title race and currently boast a two-point lead over Bayern Munich, which makes them a formidable foe for Arsenal on Tuesday. The Gunners, though, are the type to stump the stiffest competition and seem likely to do just that in the Champions League this week, even if Dortmund put up a compelling fight. -- Pardeep Cattry

Best bet: Declan Rice to have a shot on target (+160): This is a closer game than the odds suggest, as Arsenal should be favorites but a -200 line is too steep when facing the current Bundesliga leaders. But when games are close like this one, that's when big game players like Declan Rice are at their best. Without David Raya, the Gunners will need their set pieces to be on point, and that's where Rice and free kicks will make a difference. -- Charles Booth

Player to watch: Donyell Malen, Roma -- With more goals in Europe's top five leagues than anyone bar Raphinha or Kylian Mbappe, Malen is seeing the ball very big right now. Here is a forward who gets a lot of shots in the penalty area, the question for Roma on Wednesday night will be whether they can get possessions in those areas often enough. -- James BengeMan of the match: Donyell Malen, AS Roma -- 12 goals scored in 11 Serie A games, four goals scored in four Champions League matches. What can we say? He's been more than outstanding and he's a solid candidate for the MVP Serie A of the season and the Golden Boot as well. -- Francesco Porzio

Prediction: Paris Saint-Germain 3, Roma 1 -- Roma have been one of the stories of the season so far in Italy where another competitive title race is brewing; Gian Piero Gasperini's in the thick of it with a one-point lead over Inter while sitting two points behind league leaders Lazio. They do have defensive issues in Europe, though, so far conceding eight goals in four games. Reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain are the exact type of team that can exploit those weaknesses, though, which may lead to another unfavorable Champions League outing for Roma. -- Pardeep Cattry

Best bet: Donyell Malen to score (+165): With PSG's injury crisis, there will be space for Roma to create on the attacking end of things. Unfortunately, the Italian side haven't been able to hold leads when they get them, but it'll make this that much more of an interesting game. As long as he gets service, Maylen will add to his 16 goals in all competitions before PSG eventually triumphs in the match. -- Charles Booth

#1140. Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Quantum metrology promises measurement precision beyond classical limits by exploiting large-scale quantum states1,2,3,4,5,6,7, yet realizing this advantage faces two fundamental challenges: the deterministic preparation of non-trivial quantum probes8,9 and the efficient extraction of metrological information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces10,11,12. Here, we introduce quantum confocal microscopy in Fock space that addresses these challenges for a Fock-like probe state with a tightly concentrated photon-number distribution. Drawing a direct analogy between classical wave optics and quantum state evolution in a bosonic mode13,14, we construct a confocal lens system with a quantum circuit of \({\mathcal{O}}(1)\) operational depth, realizing a bidirectional transformation between a readily obtainable coherent state and this Fock-like probe state. Using a superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamics platform, we deterministically prepare focused probe states with mean photon numbers up to N = 500, achieving a 21.5 ± 1.1 dB reduction of the photon-number variance relative to a coherent state. Using the focused states for displacement sensing, we achieve a record metrological gain of 19.20 ± 0.20 dB beyond the standard quantum limit. This work establishes quantum confocal microscopy as a compact protocol that makes high-photon-number non-Gaussian Fock-like probes experimentally accessible and measurable, providing a viable route towards quantum-enhanced precision measurement, and is readily extendable to other bosonic platforms and high-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

#1139. Enzo Maresca's ref rage: Man City boss claims recent decisions are worst he has 'ever seen' as he becomes latest manager to hit out at officials

Published: 11:59 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:35 EST, 27 November 2026

Enzo Maresca has echoed Mauricio Pochettino’s punchy criticism of refereeing displays by claiming that some recent decisions against Manchester City are among the worst he has ever witnessed.

The absorbing rivalry between titans Erling Haaland and Gabriel – a battle renowned for excessive physicality - returns when City go to Premier League champions Arsenal on Sunday.

And Maresca suggested that key calls in City’s recent winless run have contributed to them falling six points behind Mikel Arteta’s leaders.

Asked whether Haaland is treated unfairly by officials, the Italian said: ‘I can see that, to be honest. I can see also more things in the last four or five games - probably since the international break.

‘I’ve never seen in my life a player touch the ball with both arms and no penalty. For instance against Brighton, (Lewis) Dunk. I never seen it in my life. If you remember, both. No penalty. The other one was like volleyball.’

The second complaint from that Brighton defeat was an appeal for handball against Lukas Vuskovic, when Diego Gomez headed into the defender’s outstretched arm. The league’s Key Match Incidents panel voted 3-2 in favour of Craig Pawson’s decision not to award a penalty for Dunk’s handball.

Maresca suggested that key calls in City’s recent winless run have contributed to them falling six points behind Mikel Arteta’s leaders

New Manchester United boss Pochettino said last weekend that with VAR, the league possesses ‘the best car but we need to drive it in the right way’ following Leny Yoro’s sending off at Liverpool.

Maresca’s analysis also partly centred on how VAR is being used as he raised Haaland’s disallowed goal against Fulham at the weekend, when the striker was adjudged to have fouled Bernd Leno and VAR stuck with the on-field decision.

‘The last game against Fulham, if you just stop (the image) when the goalkeeper has the ball there, it looks like (a foul), but the dynamic is he is not catching the ball,’ Maresca added.

‘Even the keeper does not believe that he was. Yes, there are fouls for Erling, but I can see also in the last games from the international break things that I don’t like, that for me are clear. But the referee is there, they decide, so we need to adapt.’

Haaland has talked up his enthusiasm for going up against Gabriel this week and should be reinvigorated for the challenge after cutting a forlorn figure during and after the 2-2 draw with Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

The 26-year-old appeared downbeat during media interviews immediately after the game, sparking a discussion over his current frame of mind.

Maresca insisted that the striker’s mood is in line with other players as they strive to break free of a disappointing set of performances.

‘Erling is a winner,’ the City manager said. ‘It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but it’s not just Erling, it's everyone. Don't forget that two weeks ago or three weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch (after beating Brighton in the Carabao Cup).

Asked whether Haaland is treated unfairly by officials, the Italian said: ‘I can see that, to be honest. I can see also more things in the last four or five games'

‘You can write or think many different things, but the reality is sometimes much easier: Erling is upset, like I'm upset because we're not winning games. And when we were winning games everyone was happy. But this is our job, this is football, that's why we need to maintain the balance.’

Haaland has admitted that he needs to improve in front of goal after scoring just once in his last five club games, yet Maresca believes the problems instead lie in quality consistent service.

‘I think he is gesticulating in the same way when we were winning games and he was not receiving balls,’ he said. ‘Erling is a No 9, the No 9’s live day by day for goals.

‘When we drop the opposition inside the box and he is inside the box, he is the king there. The problem is that most of the teams now, because they are so aggressive, they come higher on the pitch, so you need him also to link a little bit. We need him in different ways.

‘I'm not a magician, there is a transition here. It's normal. We have eight, nine new players, manager is new - you need time. You see at different clubs when they had transitions, how complicated it is.’

#1138. Cavan Sullivan wins MLS Young Player of the Year as league announces award winners and finalists

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the MLS Cup playoffs now in full swing, it also means that we are beginning to see who is taking home honors at the end of the season. Nashville SC have already seen Maxwell Woledzi win Defender of the Year and Bran Shwake earn Goalkeeper of the Year honors, and they have potential honorees up and down the awards docket alongside the youngest MVP finalist in league history, Cavan Sullivan, who has taken home young player of the year honors. Antoine Griezmann has also won Newcomer of the Year in only half of a season with Orlando City SC.

Check out the winners and finalists so far:

Leading Nashville SC to a record low of 25 goals conceded and tying Tony Meola's record for the most clean sheets in an MLS season with 16, Brian Schwake has taken home Goalkeeper of the Year honors by a landslide, beating out finalists Matt Turner and Roman Bürki. In only his first season as the full-time starter for Nashville, Schwake took the reins and didn't look back, also debuting for the U.S. Men's National Team due to his success. He also set club records for wins, penalty kick saves (three), save percentage (78.4%), and goals against average (0.76).

It's astounding that Eduard Lowen is playing soccer, considering what the few years have looked like for him. In March of this year, his wife Ilona died from brain cancer after they managed through her diagnosis, with Lowen taking time off from the game to support her and her family. He returned to MLS play in April, scoring in his first start of the season for St. Louis City SC, but then was traded to San Jose after the World Cup break. During that time with San Jose, he became an important part of their playoff run with one goal and three assists.

Becoming the youngest MVP finalist in league history at only 17, it should come as no surprise that Cavan Sullivan has won Young Player of the Year, beating out the Red Bull New York duo of Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti. During the World Cup break, Sullivan spent time training with the Union's MLS Next Pro side instead of taking the time off for himself, and the results showed in the second half of the season as he helped lead the Union into a playoff spot. With nine goals and 14 assists (including secondary assists), no teenager has ever been involved in more goals in a season than Sullivan, and it has also led to his first cap with the United States men's national team, where he was able to grab his first goal against Mexico. If this is the tip of the iceberg, we're in for something special, considering that this has been a banner year for young players in MLS, with more minutes being given to teenagers than ever before. The future is in good hands as the kids are leveling up each day.

With Guilherme receiving MVP votes to become a finalist for the award, it was going to take a special performance for someone else to win Newcomer of the Year, and joining Orlando City SC, Antoine Griezmann did just that. Prior to his arrival, this was a team floundering below the playoff line after moving on from manager Oscar Pareja. In only a half-season, he came in and scored 14 goals and assisted eight more as the first player ever to produce 20 goal contributions in only half a season, while turning this team into contenders. It's going to be tough in the playoffs for Griezmann to overcome the defense, but considering what he has already done with the squad, there's no reason why Orlando should be counted out with the Frenchman next to Justin Ellis.

En route to setting a points record with 77 points to win the Supporters' Shield, Nashville SC were also led by a record-setting defense that only let the ball into the back of the net 25 times in an entire campaign. That success was rewarded with all three finalists for Defender of the Year coming from Nashville, but it's their newest signing that took home the award. Joining from Norwegian club Fredrikstad ahead of the season, Woledzi didn't need much time to adjust, appearing in every regular-season match and helping Nashville build from the back to maintain possession. It was a team effort to tie the MLS clean sheet record with 17 during the season, so it's only natural for one of their defenders to get the honors this season.

#1137. Man City have a striker who will not be stopped and a defence that cannot be trusted

Manchester City surely cannot win the Champions League with a defence leaking goals and a goalkeeper making errors. But when Erling Haaland is in the team, anything seems possible.

This thrilling victory for City perfectly sums up their season: needless goals conceded, Gianluigi Donnarumma making a mistake, followed by Haaland saving the day with a winning goal.

“How can you stop Haaland?” read the headline in the local Volkszeitung newspaper on the morning of this Champions League clash. The answer is that it has been impossible for RB Leipzig.

Leipzig roll out the Red Bull carpet when they face the Norweigan. He has now scored 13 goals against them in nine matches, the most he has scored against a single team during his career. Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

#1136. Nicolò Tresoldi: Why 2027 could change everything with a likely transfer and a career-defining decision ahead

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There is a new talent in Europe who will make his name in the near future, and that's Nicolò Tresoldi. The 22-year-old is currently playing for Club Brugge and on October 13 scored three goals at San Siro against Inter, showing the world he's ready for the next step in his career. 2027 will be a pivotal year in Tresoldi's career, not only because he could be on the verge of a move to a bigger European club, but also because he may have to make a definitive decision about his international future. With Germany, Italy and Argentina all potentially in the picture, choosing which national team to represent could prove just as significant as his next club move.

When Tresoldi, the son of a former Serie A player, scored the hat-trick against Inter at San Siro, all the headlines were about his childhood and his love for AC Milan, the Nerazzurri's biggest rival, who, according to reports, are also in talks to potentially sign him in the future. But just how special is Tresoldi, and which European giants could be in the running to sign him in 2027?

Nicolò Tresoldi silences the San Siro 🤫Club Brugge stun Inter 🥶 pic.twitter.com/D8TIEn6b9C

Tresoldi was born in Cagliari, Sardinia, in 2004, during the summer months when his family would regularly spend time on the island. His connection to Sardinia stemmed from his maternal grandfather, who worked there as a golf instructor. Thanks to this family connection, they had a house on the island and would spend part of their summers there, but because of his mother's job, he moved with his family to Hannover in 2017, when he was 13.

Tresoldi, who until then had played tennis more regularly, decided to start his soccer career in the Hannover academy, where he debuted with the second team before making his first-team debut in 2022. He immediately drew interest from multiple European clubs, and in the summer of 2025 he joined Club Brugge in Belgium, his first major move as a professional soccer player. In his first season at the club, he scored 23 goals in 58 games, including four in the Champions League's league phase, and he has started his second season even better, with 15 goals in all competitions so far, including that unforgettable hat-trick against Inter in Milan.

Next year will also be the year he makes a final decision about which national team he wants to represent. Tresoldi is eligible for Germany, Italy and Argentina. In 2023, he decided to join the German U21 team, and he now intends to see out the entire cycle through the 2027 U21 European Championship, which will take place in the summer. Until then, he won't make a final decision, but both Italy coach Roberto Mancini and Germany coach Jürgen Klopp have expressed interest in calling him up.

Speaking on the topic and about Tresoldi's future, Klopp said: "It doesn't mean that he has made a decision against Germany or Italy. We don't want to put any pressure on the players. It's a sensitive matter, and we will respect whatever decision he makes, without rushing him." Mancini, on the other hand, seemed more optimistic about him choosing Italy: "I've spoken to Tresoldi myself. He needs to feel that he wants to represent our national team. Given that he was born in Italy and has an Italian father, I believe there is a possibility. We hope he makes the right choice; he knows how much he would mean to us." Argentina can also hope to call him up, as his mother is from there, and he could be included in Lionel Scaloni's squad. However, Italy and Germany are his most likely choices.

Before that, he will also be the subject of transfer rumors starting in the early months of the new year, as many top European clubs are looking for a new striker. AC Milan have to be on that list, as the Rossoneri will likely sign a new striker to play alongside Gonçalo Ramos, even though Club Brugge reportedly value him at around $50 million. At the same time, we need to monitor what Bayern Munich do in the January transfer window, as Harry Kane's injury might force the German side to change strategy in the short term. For sure, 2027 will be the year of Tresoldi, as he now focuses his attention on two moves that will shape his future.

LONDON -- To lose one elegantly-earned lead, Mr. Arteta, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose two looks like carelessness. Three days after frittering away their lead at Newcastle, Arsenal repeated in the Champions League, as Borussia Dortmund became the first team to stop Mikel Arteta's side from winning a league phase game at the Emirates Stadium.

The real impact of two points dropped tonight probably won't become clear until February and the draw for the last 16. A year ago, topping the league table set Arsenal on a favorable path to the Champions League final. There are, of course, no guarantees that they would not get that as a lower seed but a repeat finish in the top two looks unlikely, with Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain both in possession of 100% records.

Of more immediate concern for Arteta, who was unstinting in his praise of Arsenal's "brilliant performance", is that this team's very good football is not enough to overwhelm their opposition. It is worth noting, at this early juncture, that this team did position itself to potentially overwhelm the German league leaders. As is so often the case with the Gunners, we're assessing them against standards that would be considered unreasonable for 99% of teams. Usually, when you put up 2.2 xG on Borussia Dortmund and give up 0.9, you can be as pleased with your side as Arteta was in public. In private, you can rest assured that he will be as detail-obsessed as this column in attempting to explain why such sustained spells of excellence still end in a share of the points.

As at St. James' Park on Saturday night, for 45 minutes here, Arsenal were delicious, a true smorgasbord of footballing delights. Piero Hincapie popping up as an additional center forward, Christos Tzolis gliding off the left, Declan Rice barnstorming from third center back to second attacking midfielder in the space of a single pressing trigger.

Borussia Dortmund arrived in north London tied with their hosts for the fewest goals conceded in Europe's top five leagues. Niko Kovac's back five, with three robust midfielders ahead of them, looked like it should be enough to stifle the Gunners. Instead, they were overwhelmed, pulled here and there in their attempts to track position-lite red shirts.

Arsenal's excellence got the goal it deserved, a larruping strike from Viktor Gyokeres that moved one way, then the other, with such extravagance you rather wondered if the Australian cricket team had given the ball a going over beforehand. Nico Schlotterbeck seemed convinced he'd got an edge on it. Gregor Kobel looked dumbfounded. Even Gyokeres' belated donning of the Bane mask suggested he thought there had been some external force aiding him. Not so. You just hit it that well, Viktor.

From there, Arsenal had all they needed to wrap this game up in style. Their press constricted the game into the spaces where Martin Odegaard could excel. Noni Madueke was even more menacing, a player who seems to have unlocked himself in little over a month. They kept getting into the final third. They kept getting shots, too, 14 of them before the half was out. The problem was how bad those shots were. A baker's dozen and one spare and Arsenal couldn't put up a full expected goal before the break.

Too often, moves ended prematurely because someone in red fancied taking a swing from range. Eight of their first-half shots were from outside the box. Gyokeres tried a few heat checks; come the final whistle, he was as cold as the north London night. Declan Rice has evidently read Arteta saying that he should try more shots from range. The ones from outside the box, one of which really brought the oohs as it flew over the bar, weren't even his worst. Not squaring for Madueke in the first half or Gyokeres in the second really was a spurning of prime opportunities.

If this rush to shoot from range were a one-off, you could frame it as Arteta did in his post-match press conference, "a variation in relation to the opponent, the situation that you have". And yet Arsenal have been trying from range more frequently this season, from fewer than four shots per game in 2025-26 to nearly five this term, a 23% increase in shot volume from range. Against Newcastle, the proportions were lower but twice in an excellent 45 minutes, they shot when they could have worked the ball into a better spot. Arteta has spoken about unlocking the long-range potential of his team. Those who know his thinking often frame his obsession with adding "gamechangers" to his roster in terms of players who can beat a man and strike one from deep.

They still take a lower proportion of efforts from outside the box than most teams in Europe's top five leagues but most teams in Europe's top five leagues don't employ Martin Odegaard. For now, the sample size and the variation might be so small as to be explained through happenstance or circumstances rather than design. Bukayo Saka's injury has removed one of Arsenal's primary penalty-box threats from this team. His replacement, Madueke, is still honing his shot profile, if we're being generous.

There is also value to a team that faces so many low blocks proving themselves to be willing to strike from range. Fail to close down an Eberechi Eze and you might well be picking the ball out of your net soon after. Get those defenders moving out of position to close down the shot and an angle to a better opening might present itself.

It is a hard balance to strike. Tonight, Arsenal did not quite manage it: prime positions turned into subprime shots because trigger fingers got itchy.

A driving run from Joane Gadou took him away from Christos Tzolis, as the midfield busied themselves with other matters. Maximilian Beier received the ball in the box and smartly turned away from Gabriel before drilling low past Kepa Arrizabalaga. Even a defense as excellent as Arsenal's can't keep your average Premier League or Champions League opponent from clicking once. The levels are just too high.

An upswing in pressure in the final 35 minutes brought enough moments to leave Arteta baffled. "There is an element of luck here because how in hell some of the goals they haven't gone in, I don't know. Some of the days last year we hit somebody and it was an own goal.

"Quality sometimes [is missing], or [there is a] rush, or [a need] to have a bit of composure, or to read the next pass a little bit better; the execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think was really, really good."

He is not wrong. It just seems even more careless to let two points slip away because they could not quell their shot-first instincts.

#1133. From young players to women's game to the national team, how can SFA duo Maxwell and Mulholland possibly be trusted to move things forward?

Published: 13:33 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 15:30 EST, 27 November 2026

With the Scottish FA’s widely trumpeted plan to get young players more game time now lying in a ditch off the M74, it was hard not to raise a wry smile at the midweek communique from Hampden over the intention to come up with some other kind of just-as-good idea somewhere in the new year.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right,’ it closed.

Bit late for that chat, is it not? Shouldn’t that work behind the scenes have been done before the grand summit at St Andrews back at the start of September when SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell and his chief football officer Craig Mulholland announced themselves lords and saviours of the national game with their scheme to shoehorn Under-21 players – no matter how good, bad or indifferent they may be – into club sides all over the country?

It all sounded good at the time, of course, if you put your head in the clouds and daydreamed over how pretty the world might be if everyone just got along.

Handwringers nationwide fell over themselves to simper the usual platitudes over how self-interest must be sacrificed for the greater good. There was probably some kind of online petition to link hands between all 42 senior grounds for a chorus of Kumbaya.

Meanwhile, anyone who has the faintest idea of the realpolitik of Scottish football looked at what was on the table and knew it was destined for the knacker’s yard.

SFA top brass Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell flank Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli

The SFA should have been consulting their more prominent clubs before going public over what might work and what might not, moulding something that the teams which matter were willing to support.

Instead, almost half the outfits in the Premiership blew their proposals out of the water in the end.

The sound of silence from Hampden, of course, had already become deafening as they realised they’d made a pig’s ear of it. Right now, it looks like everyone is back to the drawing board.

It’s embarrassing for the SFA. It has just made Maxwell and Mulholland look like they are incapable of taking the game with them on important matters.

Naturally, though, there wasn’t a single word from Haudit or Daudit in that press release to more or less confirm a major reverse ferret is going to be required. When things go belly-up, the high heid yins at Hampden are often nowhere to be seen.

Maxwell was too busy turning his mind to other matters during the week anyway, namely the fact that Scotland will be co-hosting the Women’s World Cup with the rest of the UK in 2035.

Given that was the only actual bid, the award of the event was hardly earth-shattering, but that didn’t stop Maxwell treating it as his Next Big Thing.

Maxwell has been in position at the SFA for more than eight years but has lacked real impact

‘I think it is going to be an absolutely transformational event to host in the UK and Ireland,’ he gushed. ‘The hard work starts now in terms of legacy and impact and driving everything we can from it.’

Hmmmm. Nice as it is that he’s managed to put being custard-pied at home by a large chunk of the Premiership over youth opportunities behind him, it might be wise to take Maxwell’s words over the women’s game with a pinch of salt.

He also called Scotland going to their first World Cup in 2019 ‘transformational’. Months later, Glasgow City won their 13th straight title with a ten-goal win over Motherwell on a council-run pitch in Wishaw in front of 100 people with no shelter, no seating and no obvious way for an ambulance to gain entry should a medical emergency occur. One Motherwell player had to nick across to the attached sports centre to get a chair for an injured team-mate to sit on.

A year had passed since the national team’s qualification, but there was still no kind of plan for the £400,000 prize money that they earned.

City’s Hayley Lauder, who’d been at the World Cup in France, tweeted: ‘Just won a league title in a public park at a sports centre. Not how I envisaged the game in 2019.’

It was a message that encapsulated the catastrophic failure to build on the incredible platform France 2019 provided under Maxwell’s reign.

Scotland celebrate an Erin Cuthbert goal against Argentina in 2019 before it all turned sour

That should have been the real launchpad for the women’s game here. Instead, it turned into a toxic shambles that killed any kind of momentum.

Progress since has been nothing like what it should have been. The national team, out to reach the next World Cup in next week’s play-off against Sweden, has been mired in failure. The women’s game lives back in the shadows amid pitiful attendances and an inability – or, it sometimes seems, refusal – to sell itself.

Yet, it could all have been so different. Just remember the scene back in ‘19. Scotland have to beat Argentina to make the last 16. A TV audience of six million watched the meeting with England earlier in the campaign.

The drama as Shelley Kerr’s side let slip a three-goal lead with 16 minutes to play – eventually drawing 3-3 thanks to a stoppage-time penalty retaken after an initial save by keeper Lee Gibson – was just incredible. It was the talk of the nation the next day.

And, then, it all just died a death. The head coach Shelley Kerr eventually coughed to the fact ‘a few drinks’ had been taken before a debrief the next day that reportedly left some players in tears.

No one wanted to talk about it. No one ever has, really. Yours truly asked Glasgow City for an interview with Gibson, then Alexander, in the early stages of the following season.

Top-flight matches between teams in the SWPL regularly take place on glorified public pitches

She’d been at the centre of a major global event. There was a story to be told. City insisted all requests had to be run past the SFA and their media office pretty much made it clear it wouldn’t be happening before she had even been asked.

No one told their stories of the biggest event in the history of women’s football here. Not properly. It felt like some kind of Omerta had been put in place over it.

Kerr, inexplicably, was allowed to keep her job by Maxwell and then failed to make it to Euro 2022. Instead, that year was marked by the women’s team, with Kerr gone, threatening to take legal action against the SFA over a lack of resources – with then captain Rachel Corsie referring to ‘years of iniquity, disrespect, and, in some cases, abuse.’

Yeah, the aftermath of France 2019 was ‘transformational’ all right. It transformed the hundreds of thousands of folk compelled to watch women’s football on national TV that summer back into people who forget it even exists.

Colleagues tell me there was no scope midweek to even interview anyone in a position of power within the SFA over what should have been a Good News Story regarding 2035. Hardly ‘driving everything we can from it’, is it?

I mean, how can you trust the likes of Maxwell to harness the opportunities afforded by that event – or Euro 2028 on home soil – when reflecting upon the raging binfire France 2019 became?

Mulholland is a regular sight being entertained by football matches up and down the country

How can you trust him and Mulholland to get it right on forging pathways for young players when they made such a Horlicks of trying to implement that poorly-planned proposal for Scotland-eligible Under-21s and failed again when changing it to involve Under-23s?

There’s a far wider issue with the production of players that involves going deep into the SFA’s own workings, addressing that lack of knowledge St Mirren boss Craig McLeish talked about at the lower levels of grassroots.

Indeed, there are problems all over the SFA. With refereeing standards. With VAR. With Steve Clarke admitting he forced the top brass into ‘panicking’ before the World Cup and giving him a new four-year deal.

If Maxwell and Mulholland’s blue-eyed boy Sebastien Pocognoli doesn’t start looking like he’s got a handle on his role as Clarke’s successor as national boss after a grim start to his reign, everything points to the two of them having to go the same way as their original Youth Plan. By being binned.
