#1132. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Manchester United face defensive crisis in tough visit to Sporting

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Another week of Champions League football comes to a close on Wednesday night as plenty of teams on the top-eight or even top-24 bubble find themselves with work to do. A shock loss to Club Brugge means that there is pressure on Inter as they face Stuttgart at the San Siro; certainly, if they are to take up a top-eight berth, this is a game they are going to have to win.

Do Manchester United have such lofty aspirations? It is with the Red Devils we start, and no wonder, given their trying run of form lately. That they do have as many wins as defeats from their first four games is almost a surprise, but a difficult fixture list shows no sign of easing for Mauricio Pochettino as his side faces Sporting in Lisbon tonight.

If there was a silver lining to the very dark clouds over Manchester United on Sunday, it would have been that there is at least plenty of time to cure what ails them in the Premier League. A point from safety is a disastrous place for such an august team to be at any point in the domestic season, but when there is more than 70% of it left to play, at least the danger is not yet cataclysmic. As for the Champions League, well, United are drifting nearer to that point.

With half their games played, they have six points. Not bad, you would have to say, good enough for 17th place in the league phase. The trouble is that their remaining four games all look difficult indeed: RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at Old Trafford either side of Christmas, then a trip to a Villarreal outfit that should have plenty to play for on the final day. Tonight's visit to Sporting might be as good a shot at three points as Pochettino gets, and the Portuguese giants have three wins from four. He will not want to be trying to accrue four-plus points in three games.

It's all feeling very high stakes in league and Europe, the sort of moment when clear heads are needed. Not one for doom and gloom, or for Kobbie Mainoo to tell United's in-house channel "we're at the lowest we've ever been and no one's coming to save us." Then again, he's not wrong.

Already this club looks like it's doom-spiraling. It's on Pochettino to fix that. His first task will surely be to rustle up a defensive quartet who at least don't magnify each other's flaws. Does Matthijs de Ligt need time out to find the sharpness he so lacked against Liverpool? Can anyone fill in at left back? Diogo Dalot, still, really? Their organization will be tested against a Sporting side that attacks quickly and centrally, qualities that should terrify a backline that will likely be shielded by the slow-moving Mainoo and Youri Tielemans.

Sporting always score, their 22-game streak of goals in the group stage and league phase a record for a Portuguese club. Right now it looks like United are doomed to forever concede. This could get dicey.

In spite of what you might assume about Italian clubs, Inter's success at home and on the continent has not always been underlaid with defensive excellence. Certainly, there have been some memorable individual displays, none more so than Yann Sommer standing tall against the Barcelona onslaught, but great defense tends not to be about one player doing the spectacular over and over. After all, sometimes excellence is required because of mistakes elsewhere.

And right now mistakes are plaguing Inter across the field. Their 12 Serie A games have seen the concession of 17 goals, two in the final 10 minutes at Atalanta turning what might have been a valuable 4-2 win on the road into a chastening draw. It's the same story in the Champions League, where there have been a competition-high four errors leading to goals and another three leading to shots. Those sorts of numbers may not be very predictive, but in this case they feel indicative of a defense that has taken a step down from a level that wasn't that high to begin with.

Some of that problem lies with recruitment. It might have been time to move on from Sommer, but Josep Martinez has not proven himself to have been the ready-made replacement in the wings he might have been. Francesco Acerbi and Stefan de Vrij were similarly long in the tooth, and there was an argument for swapping out experience for experience in the form of ex-Manchester City duo Manuel Akanji and John Stones. The issue when you keep going for old guys, though, is that some of them are on the downslope (Akanji) and others can't stay fit (Stones). Being a bit too old might be an issue in midfield too.

These failings are being particularly exposed in the Champions League, where Club Brugge, Real Madrid and even Shakhtar Donetsk have ended up with good shot volume and expected goals. Domestically, Inter allow a solid 1.1 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) per game, but maybe that says more about the field in Serie A. Or maybe there's just a lot of air in four Champions League games in which 7.6 npxG has been allowed.

It might be true that, as the graphic indicates, Inter's defense has stabilized a bit of late after a bad start to the season, although it probably did not feel like that when Milan were scoring three goals off 0.62 xG. It also helps no end when the attack is firing, Francesco Pio Esposito giving Cristian Chivu every manager's favorite sort of headache. However, against a Stuttgart side that can test the best defenses -- 1.96 npxG per Bundesliga game, 2.09 in the Champions League -- that defense is going to have to get its house in order.

Has it finally clicked for Florian Wirtz? Well, maybe. The 23-year-old leads the Premier League in chances created, trails only Declan Rice for assists provided, and is one of only five players with over two expected assists from open play this season. All that, and he ranks in the top 20 for shots and in the 91st percentile for npxG. At 11 games, it might be worth considering a few caveats. Nineteen of his 33 chances created came against Brentford and Manchester United. In the match against the former, there were an awful lot of sideways passes that resulted in long-range shots from the receiver, a chance created in law if not in spirit. As for the other game, well, it was against Manchester United. Ten-man Manchester United at that.

Wirtz can still get locked out of high-leverage games against Arsenal and Manchester City. The Wirtz who, in Bayer Leverkusen colors, seemed the surest nine-figure bet in the game tended to excel whatever the opposition. For Liverpool, it has to be just right. A game that is more up and down with fewer demands on him to break down a low block. Opponents who are slightly less muscular than the Premier League average (see Manchester United). There is still a suspicion that a league as physical and fast as England's might lessen Wirtz's effectiveness, though the man himself would contend otherwise. He says he is getting used to the demands of the league.

"I can't really say that I've changed that much," he said when asked how he had adapted to life with Liverpool. "I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."

Credit also went to Andoni Iraola, who has afforded Wirtz a largely settled run as the primary creator in a 4-2-3-1. "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football," the German international said. "I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that. I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me."

Expect this good form to continue in Europe, where Wirtz has generally looked a more threatening player than he does in the Premier League. In part that's a function of the aforementioned physicality. It's probably also true that the likes of LASK, Villarreal, Qarabag and Wednesday's opponents Club Brugge would not exactly be pulling up trees in the Premier League either. A chance, then, for Wirtz to build even more momentum.

#1131. Depleted PSG attack shows vulnerability in 2-2 Champions League draw with Roma

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Have Paris Saint-Germain been defanged? It is too soon to say if injuries have laid low the Champions League's biggest beast, but on the evidence of Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Roma, there might not be quite the same fear factor when opponents find themselves face to face with the kings of Europe's jungle.

Without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue, both of whom are expected to miss most, if not all, of this season with knee injuries, there simply was not the final-third threat in PSG's ranks to keep Roma honest without the ball. That was all the more pronounced given that Ousmane Dembele was left on the bench until the penalty with which PSG took a 2-1 lead. Maghnes Akliouche, Senny Mayulu and Ferran Torres are talented forwards, the last good enough to win a World Cup final for Spain. Pair one or even two of them with the potential Ballon d'Or winners who started for PSG in the Champions League final, and the drop-off is not particularly significant.

Of course, it might be that Luis Enrique is not particularly minded to see how good his reserves could be flanking Dembele. It would make sense. The Frenchman's fitness needs careful managing at the best of times. With PSG having won their first four league-phase games, there was no pressing need to load up minutes on a player who will surely be needed in the spring. It was a similar story at the base of PSG's team, Ilia Zabarnyi preferred to Marquinhos, another who does well to hit a dozen games before Christmas. This might be a vision of the months ahead for an injury-addled PSG, but it might just be a team that has never taken the league phase particularly seriously not taking the league phase particularly seriously.

Whatever the longer-term view, on the field this evening, PSG's attack lacked the bite to keep Roma backing off. There is a good chance that any team managed by Gian Piero Gasperini might just go man-to-man whoever the opposition, but the fearlessness with which the Giallorossi hurtled around the Parc des Princes was a sure sign they weren't checking over their shoulder quite as much.

Instead, they felt empowered to push on, center back Mario Hermoso on hand to roll in the opener inside the box after an excellent run by Matias Soule. Again, the caveat to assessing how future opponents might take on PSG is that Hermoso has been box-crashing from defense all through this season. You can't be sure he wouldn't have been in the same spot even if he were marking Doue or Kvaratskhelia.

What you can know is that Roma's aggression when PSG had the ball in open play was not what cost them. Nuno Mendes' ability to blow by his man created issues, and Achraf Hakimi got his usual shots and shot assists from advanced positions. They could have beaten Roma, but aside from the fullbacks and a few darts into the area by Joao Neves, there was not much to scare Mile Svilar in the champions' lineup.

Instead, it was familiar failings that cost Roma, who might be a real dark horse for this competition when they can successfully defend a corner. Zabarnyi did not even have to win a duel to turn Mayulu's delivery home, just standing in the space between two white shirts at the near post. PSG's second, from the penalty spot, was a Roma confection too. Wesley could argue that Svilar should have been off his line quicker when Hakimi charged in behind, but did the Brazilian need to put his arms on his man at the exact moment he broke into the box? Wesley was lucky not to get a straight red.

In such favorable positions, prime PSG often blitz their opponents. This time, even with Dembele on the field, they could not get clear. Gasperini had an ace of his own on the bench, Donyell Malen sparking Roma after his introduction. A driving run and cutback from the left had PSG scrambling, Vitinha's arm blocking a shot to hand the visitors a penalty that Malen converted.

Had a third goal come, it would probably have been for Roma, Hermoso blazing over late on. There was something more in this for Roma, who remain outside the top 24 despite such impressive displays against Real Madrid, Manchester United and now the holders. As for PSG, there will be time for Luis Enrique to work out how his side dominates Europe with its attack so limited. It would appear there is work to do.

#1130. A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood. Here we identify a gut–brain sensory-motor circuit that regulates sugar ingestion in flies. We show that the brain neurons that regulate food ingestion, IN1s1, receive excitatory input from enteric sensory neurons that penetrate the foregut epithelium and detect sugars in the gut lumen during ingestion. Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal that IN1s integrate excitatory input from multiple sugar-sensing neurons, including enteric sensory neurons, and provide inhibitory output to enteric motor neurons that control the muscles at the entry of the crop—a stomach-like organ. During ingestion, IN1 activation suppresses these enteric motor neurons, relaxes the crop duct and promotes rapid transfer of food into the crop, thereby enabling sustained food intake. Together, our findings describe a gut–brain circuit that controls the motor activity of digestive tract muscles during feeding and suggest a circuit mechanism by which nutrient signals from the gut contribute to the dynamic regulation of food intake across metabolic states.

a, Schematic of the two-photon microscope setup coupled with optogenetic stimulation. A male fly is standing on top of an air-suspended spherical treadmill (PMT, photomultiplier tube, LED, light-emitting diode). b, Schematic showing the strategy used for optogenetic stimulation coupled with two-photon calcium imaging. GCaMP6s is expressed in IN1s, while the red-shifted opsin, Chrimson, is expressed in sensory neurons. c-m, Normalized (ΔF/F0) GCaMP6s fluorescence in IN1s before and after optogenetic stimulation of candidate sensory neurons: Control group (c), sugar sensing neurons: Gr5a (d), Gr43a (e), Gr64a (f), Gr64c (g), Gr64d (h), Gr64e (i), Gr64f (j), bitter sensing neurons, Gr66a (k), water sensing neurons, ppk28 (l), and mechanosensory neurons, TMC (m). The optogenetic stimulation period is indicated in a magenta-shaded area (n = 5-8 males per genotype, 3-5 trials per fly, mean ± s.e.m., stimulation duration = 1s, continuous, power = ~0.75 mW). n, Normalized peak responses of IN1s in indicated genotypes upon optogenetic stimulation (n = 5-8 males per genotype, 3-5 trials per fly, mean ± s.e.m., Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test, ns p > 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001). IN1s respond to activation of several sugar-sensing neurons, Gr43a, Gr64c, Gr64e, Gr64f, as well as neurons labelled by TMC >. Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

Arrows indicate the neurites of Gr43a midgut surface neurons (magenta) innervating the gut muscles (blue) (scale bars = 50 μm). f, Area under the curve (AUC) analysis of active Gr43a enteric sensory neuron responses to sucrose ingestion in indicated conditions: AUC (left) and AUC/ingestion duration (right). a, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (green) together with different classes of GRNs (yellow, pharyngeal GRNs; blue, sweet/water labellar GRNs; red, bitter labellar GRNs) or putative enteric afferents (magenta) in the FAFB connectome. Illustrations are generated in “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh. The front view (top) and top view (bottom) are shown. (L, left; R, right; D, dorsal; V, ventral; A, anterior; P, posterior). b-e, Heatmaps showing the connectivity network between IN1s and different classes of GRNs or putative enteric afferents (NC, no path). Heatmaps show the synaptic distance (number of hops) from each neuron to each IN1; connections require ≥5 synapses. IN1s are synaptically closer to putative enteric afferents than pharyngeal or labellar GRNs. A threshold of 5 synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. f, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (green) with different classes of PER neurons in the FAFB connectome (magenta, second-order PER; yellow, third-order PER; blue, pre-motor PER). The front view (top) and top view (bottom) are shown. (L, left; R, right; D, dorsal; V, ventral; A, anterior; P, posterior). g, Heatmap showing the connectivity network between IN1s and different classes of feeding initiation neurons. Heatmaps show the synaptic distance (number of hops) from each neuron to each IN1; connections require ≥5 synapses. IN1s are at least two synapses away from the PER-triggering second-order, third-order or motor neurons in the SEZ. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. Neurons with cell bodies in the left hemisphere are labelled with -L, and neurons with cell bodies in the right hemisphere are labelled with -R.

a, Representative heatmap showing the ROI in the crop duct during ingestion (scale bar = 25 μm). b, Normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct before and after ingestion of low (~100 mM) (left) and high (~1 M) (right) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m.). The sugar stimulus was provided ad libitum. c, Persistence of normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct during the ingestion of low (~100 mM) or high (~1 M) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m., unpaired two-tailed t-test with Welch’s correction, *p < 0.05). d, A representative image showing the ROI in the oesophagus during ingestion (scale bar=25 μm). e, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus before and after ingestion of low (~100 mM) (left) and high (~1 M) (right) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m.). The sugar stimulus was provided ad libitum. f, Persistence of normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus when flies are ingesting low (~100 mM) or high (~1 M) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m., unpaired two-tailed t-test with Welch’s correction, p = 0.18). g, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus before and after ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) in flies with indicated genotypes (n = 4-5 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m.). h, The amount of high sucrose (~1 M) entering the oesophagus is not altered when IN1s are inhibited (n = 4-5 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m.; one-way ANOVA, p = 0.78). i-j, Normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct of indicated mutant or control flies during ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) (i), and the persistence of their normalized food fluorescence signal (j). (n = 5-6 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m., one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05) k-l, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus of indicated mutant or control flies during ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) (k), and the persistence of their normalized food fluorescence signal (l). (n = 5-6 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m., one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

a-h, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (cyan, IN1-1; green, IN1-2; blue, IN1-3; red, IN1-4) with their presynaptic inputs (a, c, e, g). Anatomy of the top four presynaptic inputs to IN1-1 (b), IN1-2 (d), IN1-3 (f), or IN1-4 (h) in the FAFB brain dataset is shown. The input neurons are ordered based on their % synaptic input to IN1s. The Codex IDs of input neurons and the percentage of synaptic inputs they provide to IN1s are indicated on top of each panel. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between neurons. i, Summary of the synaptic connectivity of IN1s and their major inputs. Arrows indicate the direction of connections (from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons). Synaptic connections between IN1s are not shown in this graph. Illustrations are generated in the “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh.

a-h, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (cyan, IN1-1; green, IN1-2; violet, IN1-3; red, IN1-4) with their postsynaptic outputs (a, c, e, g). Anatomy of the top four postsynaptic outputs for IN1-1 (b), IN1-2 (d), IN1-3 (f), or IN1-4 (h) in the FAFB brain dataset is shown. The Codex IDs of output neurons and the percentage of synaptic outputs provided by IN1s are shown above each panel. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between neurons. i, Summary of the synaptic connectivity of IN1s and their major outputs. Arrows indicate the direction of connections (from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons). The six neurons (pink) shown in the bottom row (PRW.263, PRW.249, PRW.248, PRW.310, PRW.281, and PRW.274) are the crop-innervating enteric motor neurons (CEM neurons). Synaptic connections between IN1s are not shown in this graph. Illustrations are generated in the “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh.

a, IN1s are labelled by IN1>myr-GFP (green, left) and their putative postsynaptic partners revealed by trans-Tango (magenta) in the SEZ (middle) and crop duct (right) (scale bars = 50 μm). b, Representative confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the male CNS (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). c, CEM neurons (green) do not send projections to the VNC (grey) (scale bars = 25 μm). d, Confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the female brain (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). e, Synaptic terminals of CEM neurons (green) innervating the crop duct (blue) in a female fly. (scale bar = 25 μm). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes and exact sample sizes. f, g, Schematic (generated in Adobe Illustrator) summarizing the proposed gut–brain circuit and its state-dependent regulation of crop filling. In both conditions, ingested sucrose passes through the foregut, and enteric Gr43a neurons (yellow) detect nutrient arrival in the gut and relay this signal to IN1s (green) in the brain (green arrow). IN1s integrate nutrient/taste input from multiple sources and inhibit CEM neurons (magenta; red lines), which in turn control the crop duct muscles to regulate the routing of ingested food into the crop. f, Under hungry, high-sugar-concentration conditions (~1 M sucrose), the IN1s drive sustained opening of the crop duct, resulting in high crop filling (orange dots indicate ingested sucrose). g, Under fed, low-sugar-concentration conditions (~100 mM sucrose), the same circuit produces only transient opening of the crop duct, resulting in low crop filling. Dashed arrows indicate the path of ingested food through the digestive tract. The differential crop-filling outcomes across conditions reflect the IN1 circuit’s integration of nutrient and metabolic-state information (VNC = ventral nerve cord). The fly schematic is adapted from a prior publication59.

In vivo two-photon calcium imaging of enteric Gr43a neurons during sucrose ingestion. The video on the left shows the pseudocoloured GCaMP6s fluorescence (Gr43aGAL4>GCaMP6s) in the cell bodies of enteric Gr43a neurons in the HCG of a ~24-h-fasted male fly. The video on the right shows simultaneous infrared video of the same fly ingesting high-concentration sucrose (~1M). Related to Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 4.

In vivo two-photon calcium imaging of CEM neurons during sucrose ingestion. The video on the left shows pseudocoloured GCaMP6s fluorescence (CEM>GCaMP6s) in CEM neuron projections to the crop duct of a ~24-h-fasted male fly. The video on the right shows simultaneous infrared video of the same fly ingesting high-concentration sucrose (~1M); CEM activity is persistently suppressed for the duration of ingestion. Related to Fig. 4.

Optogenetic activation of CEM neurons blocks sucrose transport into the crop. The video on the left shows food fluorescence (fluorescein-labelled ~1M sucrose) in the foregut and crop duct of a ~24-h-fasted CEM>Chrimson male fly. The video on the right shows simultaneous infrared video of the same fly during ingestion. The red square indicator marks optogenetic stimulation on/off, the yellow round indicator marks food ingestion on/off; continuous CEM activation prevents sucrose entry into the crop, which resumes rapidly once optogenetic stimulation ends. Related to Fig. 5.

#1129. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#1127. Farm that became a football factory: Club where Man United, Liverpool, Man City, Leeds and Ireland legends started out is back in national Cup final... and hoping it's the first of many more glory days

Published: 16:16 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:26 EST, 27 November 2026

Gavin Whelan had been away from the domestic game for a while and hadn’t really been looking for a way back in.

The former Drogheda United and Bray Wanderers player had stepped away from the League of Ireland at 29 and his involvement in football in the past few years had been restricted to helping coach his older son Jayden’s team as they went through the age grades at Home Farm – the fourth generation of the Whelan family to come through the club.

The Whelan dynasty, with Gavin second from right beside his uncle Ronnie (centre) and Paul (seond from left)

But when it emerged the FAI were setting up a third tier, he had a chat with Brian Honohan, who had been a Shamrock Rovers teammate of his father, Paul, and they decided to put together a group that would help put Home Farm back where they belong.

This inaugural National League final in Carlisle Grounds is a step in that direction. Home Farm face Lucan United, who beat them 2-0 in Whitehall recently in the group stages. In a way, it is like the old meeting the new although the fact that two Dublin clubs are contesting the first final in a concept that was supposed to broaden the league’s base to uncharted territories will be viewed a little sceptically.

But that shouldn’t take away from what both Home Farm and Lucan are trying to do – or the sense of camaraderie and purpose that has characterised the first truncated season of the third tier.

Clubs have become comrades in what they are trying to do – right down to ensuring each visiting team would sit down for a meal after the final whistle before beginning the journey home.

‘There has been a sense that we all have to help each other, that we are all in this together,’ says Home Farm chairman Brendan Menton.

‘So, the clubs would organise something to eat for the visiting team. It meant that if Bonagee had to go back up the road to Donegal, they wouldn’t need to stop off somewhere. It was a small thing, but it has built a real sense of togetherness among all 15 clubs.’

Nicola Brannigan (second from left), Brendan Menton (centre), Richard Dunne (second right) and Gavin Peers (right)

Brendan Menton senior was one of the founders of Home Farm back in 1928

Menton is a former chief executive of the FAI, holding that position during Saipan in 2002. But his footballing roots have been in Home Farm.

Like Whelan, Menton’s family have four generations who have lined out for the famous nursery – with his two grandchildren currently part of the underage teams. And his father, Brendan senior, was one of the founding members of the club back in 1928.

The club came into existence when Leo Fitzmaurice, concerned about the lack of recreational facilities for young people in the Drumcondra and Whitehall area, decided to set up a street league.

Home Farm Road, which is a street in the locality, was one of the roads that formed a team.

‘My father was one of the founding members of the club, who were established to play in the Drumcondra and Whitehall street league. My family lived on 31 Home Farm Road, the name came from a Monastery that was on Iona Road and back a few centuries ago, every Monastery had their own home farm and that’s where the name came from.

‘The story goes that one Friday evening, some boys from the Richmond Road team, which included Don Seery, came to play Home Farm Road but their ball burst so the two teams decided to amalgamate and from that, the club was born.’

And from such uncertain beginnings grew one of the most successful schoolboy clubs in Ireland. More than 50 Irish internationals have passed through its famous nursery – from Jackie Carey and Liam Whelan to Gary Kelly and Richard Dunne.

One of the club’s greatest claims to fame was that in the opening game of the 2023 women’s World Cup, two former Home Farm players were on the pitch, one for Ireland and one for Australia – in Abbie Larkin and Mary Fowler, who grew up for a few years in Dublin.

Ireland legends Dunne, Gary Kelly in his Leeds days and inset Jackie Carey, who captained Manchester United

While it was a schoolboy club nurturing young talent that Home Farm fostered its reputation, it was elected to the League of Ireland in 1972 and three years later achieved its greatest ever success as, in an underdog story to rival Leicester winning the Premier League, they won the FAI Cup.

Menton can still list off the names of all the players for the club’s most famous day in April 1975, including a young Dermot Keely who was in the centre of defence, and Martin Murray, who at 16 was the youngest player to win a FAI Cup medal.

‘Everyone but Jack Dempsey, who was in his late 20s or 30 at the time, was 24 years of age or under. The average age of the team was just 21 and a lot of the players were younger than that, it was an incredible achievement at the time,’ he says.

It is that sort of rich and illustrious history that Whelan, Honohan and the other stakeholders want to tap into when they were looking for a pathway back into the league. Home Farm, who had an association with Everton in the latter part of the 1990s, dropped out of the league in 1999 with the franchise being taken up by Dublin City who were eventually subsumed into Sporting Fingal, both now sadly defunct.

The Everton connection came through Martin Murray and saw one of the later graduates of the schoolboy club, Richard Dunne, whose uncle Theo was a coach at Home Farm, go over to Goodison Park as a teenager.

‘I played my schoolboy football at Home Farm and got picked up to go to Everton at 15,’ Dunne remembers.

‘We didn’t have the pathway produced by the National League then. And Home Farm was considered the top schoolboy club in Dublin at the time and when scouts and English clubs came over, this was the first port of call. That’s something that probably faded away over time, but hopefully, we can get it back.’

Team captain Jack Dempsey lifted the FAI Cup for Home Farm back in 1975

There are around 30 teams at the club now, 10 of them in an underage girls section. The hope is that the likes of Larkin and Fowler can be an inspiration for the next generation.

The club will also move to a new facility in the AUL next summer, as part of the deal that was made when the construction of the Metrolink means that they have to relocate temporarily from their nursery’s home on Mobhi Road in Glasnevin.

They have also got a tie-in with neighbouring Dublin City University, links that the club will hope to deepen. The third-level institution is seen more as a GAA university, but the hope is that they can develop a soccer scholarship programme, so players from the north of the city don’t have to travel to UCD or Shamrock Rovers.

Whelan, who availed of the UCD scholarship, says it is still in the early stages, but it is one aspect that reveals the ambitions of the club.

Nicola Brannigan, who formerly worked in the FAI marketing department but is now chief executive of the club, says the relationship has developed through the inaugural season in the national league.

‘We have students from DCU doing work experience at the club, we have communications students coming in to help us with social media, there is a law student from DCU, so that is one way that the relationship has worked. And then we have a few students or DCU graduates playing for the team,’ she says.

Under former Sligo Rovers star Gavin Peers, who played with the club as a youngster, the senior team have performed above themselves at times this season, but the ambitions are such they always felt they would be in contention to win the inaugural National League.

But the season has more being about putting Home Farm back on the map. Whelan knows from personal experience what can happen when clubs in the league endure harsh times.

Having scored in the FAI Cup final for Drogheda and winning a league title with them, he was there when things went awry a couple of years later.

Home Farm have not beaten Lucan United so far this season

‘There was a lot of good people in Drogheda at the time, but it is what can happen when the economy goes south for a club and that is why what we want to build here, we want to do in a conservative and sustainable way and it is why we made sure that the senior club, and the club that we want to eventually get back in the Premier Division, is separate from the schoolboy section.’

Whelan’s youngest son Sonny is now playing at the under-eight team, the second in a fourth generation of Whelans to pass through Home Farm, stretching back to Whelan’s father Paul and uncle Ronnie and his grandfather, Ronnie senior.

But a greater claim to fame was that Whelan’s goal for Drogheda in 2005 meant that he, his father Paul, who won it with Bohemians, and his grandfather Ronnie senior were the first three generations of the same family  to win a national cup in a European league.

But it all started in Home Farm, which is why he wants to bring the club back to the big-time, especially with the club's centenary coming up in 2028.

‘We want to bring back Home Farm, by using the foundations of what made the club in the past, and its rich history,’ he says.

‘This is where I learned manners, learned discipline, learned teamwork and all of that. The club always had the right ethos and this was just a case of leaving a legacy, showing what the club is and leaving it in a better place.’

Even though there is no promotion into the First Division this season, it feels like winning the inaugural National League will serve notice of the club’s intention of returning to where they feel they belong.

#1126. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

#1125. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1123. 2026 Concacaf W Championship: What to know, how to watch as USWNT aim to punch ticket to World Cup

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Just when you think you're going to settle in for a long winter's nap, there's more high-stakes women's soccer to watch. The 2026 Concacaf W Championship paves the way to the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil and the 2028 Summer Olympics, and eight national teams from the region will play a knockout bracket starting Friday, Nov. 27.

With World Cup and Olympic berths decided along the way, fans can watch all of the 2026 Concacaf W Championship on CBS Sports Golazo Network and Paramount+.

Here's everything you need to know about the upcoming tournament:

All times Eastern -- all games will air on Paramount+

Saturday, Dec. 5 (third-place match and final)

The Concacaf W Championship is a senior women's national team championship tournament that doubles as the region's qualifier for both the World Cup and the Olympics.

This year's edition has a new format that sends teams to the 2027 World Cup and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The biggest change is the quarterfinal bracket. The top two ranked teams, the United States and Canada, earned byes into the tournament. Jamaica, Costa Rica, Mexico, Panama, Haiti, and El Salvador all earned spots through the Concacaf W Qualifiers.

Back in 2022, eight finalists were placed into two groups of four, with the top two teams in each advancing into the semifinals and clinching World Cup spots. Third-place teams were given a chance to qualify in the inter-confederation playoffs. 2022 was also the first year the competition served as both a World Cup and Olympic qualifier, but only the champion and the winner of a two-leg playoff clinched Olympic berths.

This year, the group stages are gone, and a single quarterfinal will decide who qualifies directly. In 2026, the quarterfinal winners all earn a place in the 2027 World Cup, and quarterfinal losers compete in a play-in round, with the two winners earning spots in the inter-confederation playoffs in February 2027.

The two Concacaf W Championship finalists and the third-place finisher qualify for the 2028 Summer Games. The United States are hosts of the 2028 Olympics and qualify automatically, so if they finish in the top three, the fourth-place team takes the remaining Olympic spot.

The U.S. women's national team will face El Salvador for the first time in program history. El Salvador are the USWNT's first new opponent since playing Zambia in the Olympic group stage in July 2024.

The USWNT step into the competition as reigning Concacaf W Championship winners. They've won the last three tournaments and hold a record nine all-time titles. The USWNT won all five of their games in the 2022 W Championship without conceding a goal and outscored opponents 13-0. The USWNT are 106W-1D-0L in matches against teams ranked outside of FIFA's Top 25, drawing only to Costa Rica 0-0 in July 2024 in Washington, D.C.

Manager Emma Hayes named a 23-player roster for the tournament, but recently made some changes following the 2026 NWSL Championship. Trinity Rodman, who sustained a shoulder injury, has been replaced by Jaedyn Shaw, and Shaw will be replaced by Lia Godfrey on the U-23 roster.

Kansas City Current defender Laney Rouse was also ruled out of the U-23 roster and is replaced by Denver Summit FC defender Natalie Means.

El Salvador have never qualified for a Women's World Cup and will make their debut at the Concacaf W Championship. They qualified for the tournament by winning Group F with three clean sheets against Honduras, Barbados, and Trinidad & Tobago.

Head coach Eric Acuna is still leading the group after previous investigations into alleged abusive conduct,  and he publicly criticized players just last month after losses to Paraguay.

Players are trying to move forward and are led by Brenda Ceren, who led the team with five goals, followed by Danielle Fuentes with four, during the Concacaf W Qualifiers.

#1122. USWNT qualifies for World Cup with dominant 8-0 win over El Salvador

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

World Cup qualification has been secured for the United States women's national team after defeating El Salvador 8-0 on Friday in Texas. The USWNT only needed eight minutes to take the lead via Kennedy Wesley, and then the goals started rolling with NWSL MVP Ashley Sanchez securing a first-half hat trick. Sanchez helped cap off a first half that saw the USWNT score a whopping seven times before the break.

Emma Hayes had to balance players being at different points of their season with the NWSL regular season coming to a close on Nov. 1 but that wouldn't stop them from getting off to a fast start despite the absence of key players for the match. Trinity Rodman was replaced on the roster by Jaedyn Shaw after picking up a shoulder injury but they didn't miss a beat.

Games like this one showcase the tough decisions that Hayes will need to make as Sanchez is going to do what she can to push for a spot in a crowded attack alongside Mal Swanson, Trinity Rodman, Alyssa Thompson, and Sophia Wilson. While it's a good problem to have, as Hayes looks to build a cohesive unit between now and the World Cup she'll still want to determine who the core attack is.

If they're performing like this, though, it won't matter who is starting because even both center backs got in on the fun, taking advantage of set pieces to down El Salvador in the first meeting between the two countries.

El Salvador has had a rough journey to get here with their manager Eric Acuna calling out his squad during the October international break after they lost to Paraguay. Acuna threatened to take away the players' privileges for things such as coffee while also questioning their commitment to the national team. It's a tough environment to play in, and they still tried to bring the game to the USWNT, but meeting the buzzsaw that is the second-ranked FIFA nation in the world will lead to some results like this.

Getting out of the match with qualification secured and no injuries is a job well done and while Claudia Dickey didn't have to do much in net, her return to the starting goalkeeper role for the first time since the opening match against Spain could signal that Hayes has figured out what she wants to do with her rotating cast of keepers.

Determining that would help set up a defense in front of them, and when Tierna Davidson and Wesley didn't allow a shot during the match while offering strong pressing moving forward, they could become a hard partnership to break up behind a balanced midfield. This is the biggest win so far under Hayes, and it begins the official road to Brazil.

Next up, there's still work to do as the USWNT will face Jamaica in the semifinals on Dec. 1 as they look to win the Concacaf W Championship and players fight for those coveted World Cup spots. The depth that Hayes has doesn't allow room for complacency, and Hayes will be the winner from that, as there is a lot to choose from on the squad, and they'll deservedly be among the favorites to win the World Cup in Brazil next summer.

#1121. How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

#1120. Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
